## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** 1761, carved from Hampshire County.
- **County seat:** Pittsfield.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States.
- **Religious denominations confirmed:** Congregational (Pittsfield); others not confirmed by this survey.

---

The premise that "nothing civil exists" before 1841 is **only partly correct**. Massachusetts towns were ordered to record births, marriages, and deaths as early as 1639 — independent of the statewide 1841 act. A digitized volume, **"Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, Berkshire County, 1761–1850"** (image group 004500891, 512 images, browse-only), squarely spans the pre-state-registration years. Town-clerk entries may exist for your specific town before 1841. The guide below still centers on church registers and cemetery inscriptions as requested, but the town-clerk volume should not be skipped on the assumption that nothing pre-1841 exists.

---

| Item | Details |
|---|---|
| **Pittsfield Congregational church records, 1791–1850** | Image group 004500892, 274 images, 0% indexed — browse-only at FamilySearch |
| **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** | FamilySearch collection ID 1921657, ~987,654 persons — name-searchable; may index churches in other Berkshire towns beyond Pittsfield |

**Coverage gap:** Only Pittsfield's Congregational register was confirmed by this survey. No church-record volume for other Berkshire towns or denominations (Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, etc.) was returned. The indexed statewide collection (ID 1921657) is the tool to close this gap. Since this family's town is near both the New York and Vermont borders, the specific congregation serving it was not identified — do not assume the Pittsfield Congregational register covers a distant border town.

**Coverage gap:** No specific Berkshire cemetery was named by any tool in this survey. Sexton records and burial registers were not found online and likely exist only on paper or as published transcriptions in town/county histories. Treat cemetery inscriptions as a primary source for 1820–1850, since no civil record is guaranteed before 1841.

### Town Clerk Vital Records (pre-1841)
| Item | Details |

| **Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, Berkshire County, 1761–1850** | Image group 004500891, 512 images, 0% indexed — browse-only at FamilySearch |

The delegation's premise — that nothing civil exists for 1820–1850 because Massachusetts did not require vital registration until 1841 — is only partly correct. The FamilySearch Wiki's `Massachusetts_Vital_Records` page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records) states that Massachusetts created the first **permanent, statewide** recording system in 1841 (Boston excluded until 1850), but it also states that **town-level** recording of births, marriages and deaths was ordered as early as 1639, with the original records "still found with the clerk of the town or city" — a practice that continued (unevenly) right through the colonial and early national periods, independent of the 1841 state system. Consistent with that, `volume_search` returned a digitized volume of "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records" for Berkshire County covering **1761–1850** (image group 004500891), which squarely spans the requested 1820–1841 pre-state-registration years. So town-clerk-kept vital entries may exist for this family's town before 1841, even though the statewide system does not begin until that year. The guide below still centers on church registers and cemetery inscriptions as the delegation asked, but the town-clerk volume should not be skipped on the assumption that "nothing civil exists."

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began in 1841 (Boston excepted until 1850), per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records). Town-level recording was ordered as early as 1639, at the town level, per the same page — so a town-clerk series may predate 1841 locally.
- **What exists:** A digitized volume, "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records," covering Berkshire County, 1761–1850 (image group 004500891, 512 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only). - **Gaps:** The 1820–1841 pre-state-registration years depend entirely on whether the specific town's clerk actually kept records, per the Wiki's caveat that "not all places followed the law."
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers and cemetery inscriptions (below) — the delegation's intended focus, and the only record sets confirmed by this survey to run unbroken across 1820–1850 regardless of town-clerk compliance.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational confirmed for Pittsfield via the "Church Records (Congregational)" volume, 1791–1850 (image group 004500892, 274 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only). The statewide indexed collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection ID 1921657, ~987,654 persons) also covers the period and may include other Berkshire towns.

The statewide "Massachusetts, Church Records" collection (1921657) is the index that may fill this gap.

- **Major cemeteries:** Not confirmed by this survey — no tool result named specific cemeteries in Berkshire County.

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Civil parish:** Billy, barony of Lower Dunluce (part in Carey barony), poor law union of Coleraine, County Antrim — containing the post town of Bushmills.
- **Denominations present:** Presbyterian, Covenanter, Wesleyan Methodist, Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic (Coleraine district). Knowing which congregation your family actually attended is essential before searching any register.

---

## Record Types Available

### Church Records
The most important source for a person born c.1825, since civil registration did not begin until decades later.

**What was located online:**
Two digitized volumes covering **Ballylinny** (a townland inside Billy civil parish) were found on FamilySearch — full-text searchable but not name-indexed:

The FamilySearch Wiki page for Billy parish lists subsections for Presbyterian, Church of Ireland, Catholic, Methodist, and Covenanter records, but all are currently empty of parish-specific detail. The dedicated [Ireland Presbyterian Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Presbyterian_Church_Records) wiki page could not be fully retrieved in this survey — checking it directly is recommended.

**General Presbyterian context:** Presbyterian settlement in Ulster dates to 1605; average register start date across Ireland is c.1830, with many beginning later. Burial registers are less common. The congregation serving Bushmills/Billy may be identified through PRONI's "Guide to Church Records."

---

### Civil Registration
- **Births & deaths:** Registration began **1864** — no civil birth record exists for someone born c.1825.
- **Protestant marriages:** Registered from **1845**; all marriages registered from 1864.
- **Where held:** Post-1864 Northern Ireland civil records are with **GRONI** (General Register Office Northern Ireland).

---

### Land / Tax Records (Census Substitutes)
These are the primary indirect sources for placing a family in a townland before civil registration:
- **Tithe Applotment Books (c.1820s):** Cover landholders in this period — directly relevant to a family present before 1825.
- **Griffith's Valuation (c.1840s):** Property tax survey; a Valuation revision series volume for Ballylinny, Billy (1867–1881, image group 004689599, 76 images, browse-only) was found on FamilySearch.
- General Irish repositories for originals are PRONI (Belfast) and the National Archives of Ireland (Dublin), though no tool result confirmed which specifically holds Billy parish's originals.

### School Records
- **Deffrick National School Girls** (image group 008682995_005_M94W-68Y, 50 images, browse-only): Covers Billy parish from April 1867 — useful only for the tail end of the target period and later.

---

### Census Records
No census holding for Billy parish in this period (1780–1870) was confirmed by this survey. Most pre-1901 Irish census returns were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire in Dublin.

Not located for Billy parish specifically. The 1922 fire destroyed many original probate records nationally; substitute abstract collections (Betham, Crossle, Thrift Abstracts — available via FindMyPast) exist as Ireland-wide alternatives.

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **County:** Cork, in the province of Munster, formed as a shire county in 1606.
- **County seat:** Cork City (a separate jurisdiction within the county, documented from 1185).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic and Church of Ireland (Anglican) are both documented as present.
- **Key historical event:** The Great Famine (beginning 1845) overlaps the end of this period and drove heavy emigration from Cork's ports.

---

## Boundary Changes
County Cork was stable through the 1830s–1840s (formed 1606, no subdivision recorded). Cork City is a distinct jurisdiction within the county. No boundary changes affecting the target period were found.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Bad news:** Civil registration did **not exist** in the 1830s–1840s. Statewide civil registration of births, deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages began **1 January 1864**; non-Catholic marriages were registered from **1845** only.
- **What to do instead:** Use church records (see below).

### Church Records
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic; Church of Ireland (Anglican).
- **Record types:** Catholic registers record baptisms and marriages (rarely burials). Many Cork parishes' registers begin in the 1810s–1830s — survival for an 1830s ancestor is **parish-dependent**.
- **Where held:**
  - **Catholic registers:** The National Library of Ireland holds free online microfilm/digital images up to 1880.
  - **Church of Ireland registers:** Representative Church Body Library and local custody.

### Census Records & Substitutes
- **National census:** Nearly all pre-1901 Irish censuses were **destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire** — no surviving census for this period.
- **Census substitutes:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists occupiers of tithe-liable land — the principal census substitute for the 1830s.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s):** Lists every householder; substitutes for the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses.

### Land & Tax Records
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Covers the target decade; can place a family on specific land in Cork.
- **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s):** Slightly post-dates the target period but can corroborate where a family was located just after emigration.

### Immigration / Emigration Records
- **Relevant ports:** Cork ports (Cobh/Queenstown).
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests from Famine-era departures, often listing whole family groups including infants and young children.

### Probate & Wills
- Many Irish wills and government records were lost in the 1922 Four Courts fire (national loss — Cork-specific survival is unconfirmed).

### Cemetery Records
- Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is available as a general resource; Cork-specific coverage not confirmed by this survey.

### Newspapers
- Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is available as a general resource; Cork-specific holdings not confirmed by this survey.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland | Catholic parish register images (up to 1880) | Free online |
| Representative Church Body Library | Church of Ireland registers | Physical / by inquiry |
| General (FamilySearch Wiki) | Tithe Applotment Books, Griffith's Valuation guidance | See FamilySearch catalog |

> **Note:** The collection-search tools used for this survey returned empty results for the Cork place string, which likely reflects a tool lookup gap rather than an actual absence of digitized records. Treat this repository list as incomplete and verify directly via the FamilySearch catalog or the FamilySearch Wiki for County Cork.

---

## Known Record Losses
The **1922 Four Courts fire** in Dublin destroyed most pre-1901 census returns and many wills and government records nationwide. The key **substitutes** for Cork research are:
- Tithe Applotment Books → replaces the census for the 1830s
- Griffith's Valuation → replaces the destroyed 1841/1851 censuses
- Church registers → replaces absent civil vital records

---

## Research Tips
1. **Start with Roman Catholic parish registers** via the National Library of Ireland's free online images (up to 1880). Coverage varies by parish, so identify which Cork parish your ancestor likely belonged to first.
2. **Search the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** to place the family on specific land during the target decade.
3. **Check Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s)** as a follow-up to see if the family was still there just before or after emigration.
4. **Search passenger manifests** from Cork ports (Cobh/Queenstown) if the ancestor emigrated during the Famine — these lists often name whole families, including young children.
5. Because civil registration didn't start until 1864, **church registers are the only source for births, marriages, and deaths** in the 1830s–1840s.

---

In short: for a County Cork ancestor in the 1830s–1840s, there are **no government birth/marriage/death certificates** — Ireland didn't start civil registration until 1864. Your primary sources are **Catholic or Church of Ireland parish registers**, the **Tithe Applotment Books** (land/tax lists standing in for the lost census), and **Griffith's Valuation** for the early 1850s. If the ancestor emigrated during the Famine, **passenger lists from Cork's ports** can help. The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most earlier census records nationwide, making these substitutes essential.

A research plan can be built from this guide to prioritize which record sources to search first for your specific ancestor.

Cork is a county in southern Ireland, and this survey covered roughly the 1830s and 1840s, just before and into the start of the Great Famine. For that time and place there are no government-issued birth, marriage or death certificates at all, since Ireland did not start civil registration until 1864 (1845 for some marriages) — instead, the main sources are Roman Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers, plus two land/tax listings, the Tithe Applotment Books (1823-1837) and Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s), which stand in for the national censuses that were later destroyed in a 1922 fire in Dublin; if the ancestor emigrated during the Famine, passenger lists from Cork's ports can also help, and these list whole families including small children. ---

## Locality Guide: Lincolnshire, England (1750–1800)

**Focus:** Christenings and marriages in the pre-civil-registration era, when parish registers are the primary source.

### Key findings:

- **Original registers** are held at **Lincolnshire Archives**. FamilySearch's free indexes for this period are partial legacy copies — no longer updated or corrected — and most digitized Lincolnshire images must be **browsed page by page** (no name search available).
- **Bishop's transcripts** (duplicate copies of registers) are a valuable substitute when an original register is missing or damaged.
- **Findmypast** (subscription) offers denser indexed coverage for Lincolnshire than FamilySearch's free index.
- Other useful supplements: **poor-law/settlement papers** and **apprenticeship records**, especially where a christening or marriage entry is missing.
- **Calendar change warning:** England adopted the Gregorian calendar in **September 1752**, which can make dates around that year ambiguous.
- From **1754**, marriage entries became more detailed than earlier entries (Hardwicke's Marriage Act).

### Recommended next step:
Identify which specific Lincolnshire parish or ancestor to search first so a targeted research plan can be built.

Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records

Great Britain, Births and Baptisms, 1571-1977 (FamilySearch) is also a Legacy Collection, incomplete, no further corrections. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Great_Britain,_Births_and_Baptisms_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records

England Marriages, 1538-1973 and Great Britain, Marriages, 1797-1988 (FamilySearch) are both Legacy Collections — partial indexes, incomplete, no further corrections. Sources: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Marriages_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Great_Britain,_Marriages_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records

England, Deaths and Burials, 1538-1991 and Great Britain, Deaths and Burials, 1778-1988 (FamilySearch) are both Legacy Collections — partial indexes, incomplete, no further corrections. Sources: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Deaths_and_Burials_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Great_Britain,_Deaths_and_Burials_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records

Lincolnshire records are organized by ancient parish, not by the modern county — volume_search shows 1750-1800 Lincolnshire parish register volumes almost entirely as browse-only images (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable), filed under the individual parish (e.g. Old Somerby, North Hykeham, Kirkby Green, Metheringham), so plan to browse register images parish by parish rather than rely on a single county-wide name search.

Lincolnshire was historically divided into the Parts of Holland, Kesteven, and Lindsey, each with its own wapentakes — a record described as being in one 'Part' is still within the same county archive (Lincolnshire Archives) but catalogued under that division.

After 1753 (Hardwicke's Marriage Act), Church of England marriage registers switched to a printed form giving residence, marital status, banns/licence, and witnesses — earlier entries (pre-1754) in this 1750-1800 window will be sparser.

England adopted the Gregorian calendar in September 1752; dates just before that change, and pre-1752 dates between 1 January and 24 March, may be double-dated (e.g. 16 February 1696/7) — watch for this convention in any earlier material referenced alongside the target period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England parishes (the established church, holding registers from 1538 by national order per "England Church Records", https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records) covered most of the population in 1750-1800; nonconformist congregations (Methodist, Baptist, Independent, Quaker, and a smaller Roman Catholic presence, per the county page's later tabulation) also existed, though pre-1837 non-Anglicans were generally required to marry in the Church of England (exceptions: Jews and Quakers), per the same page.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with FamilySearch's free indexed collections ("England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," collection 1473014; "England Marriages, 1538-1973," collection 1473015; "England, Deaths and Burials, 1538-1991," collection 1473016) since they are free and partially name-indexed, but treat every hit as unverified given their Legacy-collection status (see quirks); then move to Findmypast's county-specific "Lincolnshire Parish Registers, 1538-1911" and "Lincolnshire Marriages and Banns, 1754-1837" for denser county coverage; only then browse the un-indexed FamilySearch volumes (e.g. image group 007565995_001_M923-LM6 for Old Somerby baptisms/burials 1730-1767) image by image for the specific parish.
- Search both the Church of England parish register and its Bishop's Transcript for the same parish and years, since "either may contain entries missing from the other" (England Church Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).
- If the target ancestor is not found in the expected parish, search neighboring parishes and nonconformist registers — before 1837 non-Anglicans other than Jews and Quakers were generally required to marry in the Church of England (England Church Records).
- Watch for the 1752 calendar change (11 days dropped in September 1752, New Year moved from 25 March to 1 January) and double-dating of pre-1752 dates between 1 January and 24 March (England Church Records).
- After 1754 (Hardwicke's Marriage Act), expect printed-form marriage entries giving residence, marital status, banns-or-licence, and witness names — richer than pre-1754 entries (England Church Records).
- Treat 110-parish coverage claims (e.g. the Joiner Marriage Index) as partial — confirm whether the specific parish of interest is one of the 110 before relying on it as a negative result.

This survey covered Lincolnshire, England for the years 1750 to 1800, the era before England's first national census or official birth-marriage-death registration, when the main surviving record of a family's christenings and marriages is the handwritten register kept by each parish church. Those original registers are kept at Lincolnshire Archives, and FamilySearch's free online indexes for this period are only partial "legacy" copies that are no longer updated or corrected, while most of the digitized record images for Lincolnshire parishes from this era have no name search at all and must be browsed page by page; useful substitutes for a missing baptism or marriage include the bishop's duplicate copies of the registers, poor-law and settlement papers, and apprenticeship records, and a Lincolnshire-specific subscription site (Findmypast) offers denser indexed coverage than the free index. One practical warning for this period is that England changed its calendar in September 1752, which can make dates near that year confusing, and from 1754 marriage entries became more detailed than before.

Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records

Great Britain, Births and Baptisms, 1571-1977 (FamilySearch) is also a Legacy Collection, incomplete, no further corrections. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Great_Britain,_Births_and_Baptisms_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records

England Marriages, 1538-1973 and Great Britain, Marriages, 1797-1988 (FamilySearch) are both Legacy Collections — partial indexes, incomplete, no further corrections. Sources: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Marriages_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Great_Britain,_Marriages_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records

England, Deaths and Burials, 1538-1991 and Great Britain, Deaths and Burials, 1778-1988 (FamilySearch) are both Legacy Collections — partial indexes, incomplete, no further corrections. Sources: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Deaths_and_Burials_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Great_Britain,_Deaths_and_Burials_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records

Lincolnshire records are organized by ancient parish, not by the modern county — volume_search shows 1750-1800 Lincolnshire parish register volumes almost entirely as browse-only images (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable), filed under the individual parish (e.g. Old Somerby, North Hykeham, Kirkby Green, Metheringham), so plan to browse register images parish by parish rather than rely on a single county-wide name search.

Lincolnshire was historically divided into the Parts of Holland, Kesteven, and Lindsey, each with its own wapentakes — a record described as being in one 'Part' is still within the same county archive (Lincolnshire Archives) but catalogued under that division.

After 1753 (Hardwicke's Marriage Act), Church of England marriage registers switched to a printed form giving residence, marital status, banns/licence, and witnesses — earlier entries (pre-1754) in this 1750-1800 window will be sparser.

England adopted the Gregorian calendar in September 1752; dates just before that change, and pre-1752 dates between 1 January and 24 March, may be double-dated (e.g. 16 February 1696/7) — watch for this convention in any earlier material referenced alongside the target period.

# Locality Guide: Lincolnshire, England (1750-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Lincolnshire is an ancient maritime county (FamilySearch dates it +1086/+1801 as a pre-1801 unit, then "Lincolnshire, England, United Kingdom" +1801/ onward); boundaries were stable through 1750-1800.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Lincoln.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England, United Kingdom.
- **Population during period:** This survey's place_population call returned no data for Lincolnshire for 1750-1800; not confirmed by this survey.
- **Internal divisions:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Lincolnshire, England Genealogy", https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Lincolnshire,_England_Genealogy), Lincolnshire contained 620 parishes (plus part of another and 43 extra-parochial places) and was divided into the Parts of Holland, Kesteven, and Lindsey, each with several wapentakes.
- **Religious denominations:** The same page's 1851 figures (the earliest tabulated) show the county dominated by the Church of England (657 places of worship), with Wesleyan Methodists (462), Primitive Methodists (221), several Baptist variants, Independents, Quakers, Unitarians, and 13 Roman Catholic chapels also present — a spread of nonconformity worth checking against for 1750-1800 ancestors, bearing in mind these figures are from 1851, decades after the target period.
- **Key historical events:** Not confirmed by this survey beyond the above.

## Boundary changes
Lincolnshire's county boundaries were unchanged across 1750-1800. FamilySearch's `place_search_all` records only a later top-level jurisdictional relabeling, from "Lincolnshire, England" (+1086/+1801) to "Lincolnshire, England, United Kingdom" (+1801/) — a naming/jurisdiction-tier change at the formation of the United Kingdom in 1801, not a territorial one, and it falls just after this project's window. Records for the target period should be sought under the parish and the Parts (Holland, Kesteven, Lindsey) as they existed throughout.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration of births, marriages and deaths for England and Wales began 1 July 1837 (FamilySearch Wiki, "England Civil Registration", https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration). This postdates the 1750-1800 target window entirely — it is background only, not a source for this period.
- **What exists for 1750-1800:** None at the civil-registration level; church (parish) registers are the primary vital-event source for this period (see Church records below).
- **Where held:** N/A for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church of England parish registers of baptism, marriage and burial, and nonconformist registers, per the Church records section below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England parishes (the established church, holding registers from 1538 by national order per "England Church Records", https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records) covered most of the population in 1750-1800; nonconformist congregations (Methodist, Baptist, Independent, Quaker, and a smaller Roman Catholic presence, per the county page's later tabulation) also existed, though pre-1837 non-Anglicans were generally required to marry in the Church of England (exceptions: Jews and Quakers), per the same page.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages (including banns registers, kept separately from 1754 onward after Hardwicke's Marriage Act), and burials, held at the parish level. Duplicate copies ("Bishop's Transcripts") were sent annually to the diocese from 1598 until most parishes stopped around 1870 — search both the parish register and its Bishop's Transcripts, as either may contain entries missing from the other.
- **Where held — online:** FamilySearch's indexed collections "England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975" (collection 1473014), "England Marriages, 1538-1973" (collection 1473015), and "England, Deaths and Burials, 1538-1991" (collection 1473016) cover the period nominally, but all three (and their "Great Britain" counterparts) are Legacy Collections — partial indexes assembled by 2010, with no further records or corrections added (see quirks). FamilySearch's own volume-level holdings for Lincolnshire 1750-1800 (via `volume_search`) are overwhelmingly browse-only images, not name-indexed (see Available record types below and Repository guide).
- **Where held — physical:** Original Lincolnshire parish registers and Bishop's Transcripts are deposited at Lincolnshire Archives (http://www.calmview.eu/lincolnshirearchives/calmview/default.aspx), per the Lincolnshire county Wiki page; nonconformist registers are mostly at The National Archives, per "England Church Records."

- **Language:** English throughout, per all pages read.

- **Federal/national census:** The first UK census was 1801, outside the 1750-1800 window; the "England and Wales Census" collections at FamilySearch (indexed and imaged) begin at 1841 per "England Online Genealogy Records." Not applicable to 1750-1800 beyond this background note.

- **Search order:** Start with FamilySearch's free indexed collections ("England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," collection 1473014; "England Marriages, 1538-1973," collection 1473015; "England, Deaths and Burials, 1538-1991," collection 1473016) since they are free and partially name-indexed, but treat every hit as unverified given their Legacy-collection status (see quirks); then move to Findmypast's county-specific "Lincolnshire Parish Registers, 1538-1911" and "Lincolnshire Marriages and Banns, 1754-1837" for denser county coverage; only then browse the un-indexed FamilySearch volumes (e.g. image group 007565995_001_M923-LM6 for Old Somerby baptisms/burials 1730-1767) image by image for the specific parish.

Locality guide saved to **loc_001**. Here is the full report from the subagent:

---

**Württemberg, Germany — Lutheran Church Records Locality Guide, 1780–1830**

**Jurisdiction & Historical Context**

Württemberg (the historical duchy/kingdom, 1495–1871, now northern and central Baden-Württemberg) had **no civil registration** during 1780–1830. Official civil vital registration did not begin in Württemberg until **1876**. For this period, the **Lutheran parish registers are the only direct record** of a baptism or marriage.

**Key Record Types**

- **Parish baptism registers (Taufbücher)** — the primary source for the period; list child's name(s), date, parents, witnesses, and sometimes sponsors.
- **Parish marriage registers (Heiratsbücher)** — record the groom, bride, their parents, and witnesses.
- **Family registers (Familienbücher)** — introduced after **1808**, grouping an entire household's births, marriages, and deaths on a single folio. These become an important supplement alongside the classic series registers.

**Repositories**

- **Landeskirchliches Archiv Stuttgart** — the Lutheran regional church archive; holds the original parish books and is the official repository.
- **Individual parishes** — some congregations still retain their own books locally.
- **FamilySearch** — digitized images of many Württemberg parish registers are available, mostly browse-only (not name-indexed), free of charge. An indexed collection begins around **1818**.
- **Archion** (subscription) — a major browse-only platform for German Protestant church books, strong Württemberg holdings.
- **Ancestry** (subscription) — also carries some Württemberg Lutheran material.

**Access Strategy**

Because most volumes are **not name-indexed**, you will need to browse images page by page. The recommended order is:
1. Start with free, already-indexed FamilySearch material (especially the post-1818 indexed collection).
2. Then move to Archion and Ancestry for browse-only volumes.
3. Contact the Landeskirchliches Archiv Stuttgart if a specific parish volume cannot be located online.

**Critical Note on Two Given Names**

It was **standard practice** in Württemberg for a baptized child to receive two or more given names, with the **second name used in daily life** (and in later records). A person who appears as a single name in later documents may be the very same child baptized under two names. The **baptism entry is the authoritative form** of the full name, not later records.

---

**Next Step:** Build a research plan working through the identified Württemberg parish register volumes, beginning with the indexed FamilySearch collection before moving to browse-only images on Archion and Ancestry.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The standard place "Württemberg" covers +1495/+1871 as a country/duchy-then-kingdom of the Holy Roman Empire and then the German Confederation/German Empire; it became the state "Württemberg, Germany" in 1871 and merged into Baden-Württemberg in 1945-1951 (place_search_all).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Stuttgart.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Holy Roman Empire until 1806, then the Kingdom of Württemberg (independent sovereign state) through 1871, then the German Empire.
- **Population during period:** No Württemberg-specific population series was returned; place_population returned only country-level German estimates (c. 18,000,000 in 1800 rising to c. 28,000,000 in 1830) and FamilySearch's German-wide indexed-birth-record counts (29.2 million for 1750-1800; 35.3 million for 1800-1850) — this survey could not confirm Württemberg's own population figures.
- **Religious composition:** The target family is Lutheran (Evangelisch); Württemberg was predominantly Lutheran, with a Catholic minority under the Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Key historical events affecting records:** The Napoleonic era (1792-1815) brought French civil registration to areas west of the Rhine, but Württemberg (east of the Rhine) returned to church-record-only practice after Napoleon's defeat; Württemberg also introduced family registers (Familienbücher) in local Lutheran parishes after 1808, consolidating family vital data on single pages (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Civil_Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Economy/ethnic composition:** Not stated by any tool result in this survey; not confirmed.

## Boundary changes
- The FamilySearch Catalog and Historical Records index places under their 1871 (German Empire / Meyers Gazetteer) names, which predates and spans the 1780-1830 target period without a boundary change to the "Württemberg" jurisdiction itself during this window (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Württemberg,_Germany_Genealogy).
- In 1945-1951 Württemberg merged with Baden and Hohenzollern into modern Baden-Württemberg; this affects where records are archived today, not where they were created in 1780-1830 (place_search_all).
- No boundary change internal to Württemberg during 1780-1830 was identified by this survey; a specific parish's affiliation can still have shifted between neighboring secular/church jurisdictions and should be checked against that parish's own church-record inventory.

args.guideSection:
### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration across the whole German Empire, including Württemberg, began 1 January 1876 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Civil_Registration). This postdates the 1780-1830 target window entirely, so civil registration is not a source for this family's baptisms/marriages.
- **What exists:** None for 1780-1830 in Württemberg; Württemberg was east of the Rhine and did not adopt the Napoleonic-era civil registration some western German territories used 1792-1815 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Civil_Registration).
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Lutheran church (parish) records are the primary source for the entire target period — see Church records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Lutheran (Evangelisch) was the majority faith; Catholic minority under the Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (Taufen), marriages (Heiraten), burials (Begräbnisse), confirmations (Konfirmationen), and — distinctively common in Württemberg and Baden after 1808 — family registers (Familienbücher) listing a couple and all their children with birth/confirmation/marriage/death dates on one page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Catalog (digitized images, variable restrictions); the Landeskirchliches Archiv Stuttgart (Württemberg's Lutheran regional church archive) via Archion (subscription, https://www.archion.de/de/archive-in-archion/baden-wuerttemberg/landeskirchliches-archiv-stuttgart/); also indexed at Ancestry (subscription, "Württemberg, Germany, Lutheran Baptisms, Marriages, and Burials, 1500-1985," https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61023/). FamilySearch's own "Germany, Württemberg, Catholic and Lutheran Church Records, 1818-1915" collection (id 4132030, 64,917 people) covers only from 1818 onward, so it captures only the later part of the target window.
- **Gaps:** No FamilySearch-indexed Lutheran collection was found covering 1780-1818 specifically by name; volume_search returned numerous individual Württemberg parish volumes spanning parts of 1780-1830 (baptism, marriage, burial registers for Cannstatt, Calw, Untersontheim, Pflummern, Klosterreichenbach, etc.) but almost all are browse-only or low-percent indexed — Archion (subscription) is the most complete single online destination for original Württemberg Lutheran church-book images across this period.
- **Language:** German (Protestant parish records in Württemberg were kept in German, not Latin, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records); be prepared for old German (Kurrent) handwriting.

### Census records
- **National/state census:** This survey found no Württemberg-specific census collection; the Germany_Census wiki page lists documented census programs only for Mecklenburg-Schwerin, Prussian Saxony, Schleswig-Holstein (under Danish rule), and Lübeck — none for Württemberg — so a Württemberg census for 1780-1830 is not confirmed by this survey (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Census).
- **Substitute for population counts:** Family registers (Familienbücher, see Church records) and tax/citizen lists effectively substitute for census enumeration in Württemberg during this period.
- **Access:** Not applicable — no collection identified.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (Testamente), estate inventories (Inventur- und Teilungsakten), guardianship records; most ordinary farmers, merchants and artisans did not own their land outright and so did not leave probate records in the usual sense (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Probate_Records).
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for this family; probate records should be sought only if a landholding or inheritance dispute is independently suspected.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch's catalog item "Germany, Württemberg, Schwäbisch Hall, Probate Records, 1803-1929" (id 1475994, 0 indexed persons — browse-only) is the only Württemberg-specific probate collection this survey found; FamilySearch holds relatively few German probate records overall, so originals are mainly at local/state archives (Amtsgericht, Staatsarchiv) (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Probate_Records).

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by this survey; no Württemberg-specific Land_and_Property wiki page content was returned beyond the generic Germany page.
- **Types:** Erbkaufverträge (inheritance sales), Lehnscheine (deeds), Verschreibungen (bonds), Pachtcontracte (leases) — recorded with the lower court rather than a land registry, since most farmers held use-rights rather than outright ownership (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Land_and_Property​).
- **Where held:** Almost none microfilmed; 19th-century land records are generally at state archives, pre-1800 records with the archives of the noble family holding lordship over the land (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Land_and_Property). volume_search found 19 land-record volumes for Württemberg 1780-1830, all browse-only.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Napoleonic Wars (1805-1815), in which Württemberg (as a Napoleonic ally/kingdom) fielded its own army; Württemberg kept its own military establishment separate from Prussia's even after 1867 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Military_Records).
- **Record types:** Military parish/garrison church records (Kirchenbücher, from 1672), personnel files, officer rolls — FamilySearch's German military holdings are sparse, hard to read, and largely unindexed.
- **Where held:** No centralized archive; Württemberg kept its own records (surviving holdings not named by any tool result in this survey) — this survey did not confirm their repository.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves are listed generically for Germany in external_links_search results (https://billiongraves.com/search#country=Germany) but no Württemberg-specific cemetery collection or count was returned.
- **Physical records:** Burial registers (Begräbnisse) are part of the Lutheran church-book series described under Church records, not separate sexton registers, for this period.

### Newspaper records

---

The survey covered Württemberg, Germany (the historical kingdom/duchy that existed from 1495 to 1871, encompassing the modern-day northern and central parts of Baden-Württemberg) for the years 1780 to 1830, focusing on Lutheran church baptism and marriage records. Most of these old parish books have been photographed and are listed online through FamilySearch and the subscription sites Archion and Ancestry, but the great majority can only be browsed page by page rather than searched by name, and the official repository for the originals is the Lutheran regional church archive in Stuttgart; local parishes themselves may also still hold some books directly. # Locality Guide: Württemberg, Germany (Lutheran church-book baptisms and marriages) (1780-1830)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The standard place "Württemberg" covers +1495/+1871 as a country/duchy-then-kingdom of the Holy Roman Empire and then the German Confederation/German Empire; it became the state "Württemberg, Germany" in 1871 and merged into Baden-Württemberg in 1945-1951 (place_search_all).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Stuttgart.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Holy Roman Empire until 1806, then the Kingdom of Württemberg (independent sovereign state) through 1871, then the German Empire.
- **Population during period:** No Württemberg-specific population series was returned; place_population returned only country-level German estimates (c. 18,000,000 in 1800 rising to c. 28,000,000 in 1830) and FamilySearch's German-wide indexed-birth-record counts (29.2 million for 1750-1800; 35.3 million for 1800-1850) — this survey could not confirm Württemberg's own population figures.
- **Religious composition:** The target family is Lutheran (Evangelisch); Württemberg was predominantly Lutheran, with a Catholic minority under the Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Key historical events affecting records:** The Napoleonic era (1792-1815) brought French civil registration to areas west of the Rhine, but Württemberg (east of the Rhine) returned to church-record-only practice after Napoleon's defeat; Württemberg also introduced family registers (Familienbücher) in local Lutheran parishes after 1808, consolidating family vital data on single pages (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Civil_Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Economy/ethnic composition:** Not stated by any tool result in this survey; not confirmed.

## Boundary changes
- The FamilySearch Catalog and Historical Records index places under their 1871 (German Empire / Meyers Gazetteer) names, which predates and spans the 1780-1830 target period without a boundary change to the "Württemberg" jurisdiction itself during this window (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Württemberg,_Germany_Genealogy).
- In 1945-1951 Württemberg merged with Baden and Hohenzollern into modern Baden-Württemberg; this affects where records are archived today, not where they were created in 1780-1830 (place_search_all).
- No boundary change internal to Württemberg during 1780-1830 was identified by this survey; a specific parish's affiliation can still have shifted between neighboring secular/church jurisdictions and should be checked against that parish's own church-record inventory.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration across the whole German Empire, including Württemberg, began 1 January 1876 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Civil_Registration). This postdates the 1780-1830 target window entirely, so civil registration is not a source for this family's baptisms/marriages.
- **What exists:** None for 1780-1830 in Württemberg; Württemberg was east of the Rhine and did not adopt the Napoleonic-era civil registration some western German territories used 1792-1815 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Civil_Registration).
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Lutheran church (parish) records are the primary source for the entire target period — see Church records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Lutheran (Evangelisch) was the majority faith; Catholic minority under the Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (Taufen), marriages (Heiraten), burials (Begräbnisse), confirmations (Konfirmationen), and — distinctively common in Württemberg and Baden after 1808 — family registers (Familienbücher) listing a couple and all their children with birth/confirmation/marriage/death dates on one page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Catalog (digitized images, variable restrictions); the Landeskirchliches Archiv Stuttgart (Württemberg's Lutheran regional church archive) via Archion (subscription, https://www.archion.de/de/archive-in-archion/baden-wuerttemberg/landeskirchliches-archiv-stuttgart/); also indexed at Ancestry (subscription, "Württemberg, Germany, Lutheran Baptisms, Marriages, and Burials, 1500-1985," https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61023/). FamilySearch's own "Germany, Württemberg, Catholic and Lutheran Church Records, 1818-1915" collection (id 4132030, 64,917 people) covers only from 1818 onward, so it captures only the later part of the target window.
- **Gaps:** No FamilySearch-indexed Lutheran collection was found covering 1780-1818 specifically by name; volume_search returned numerous individual Württemberg parish volumes spanning parts of 1780-1830 (baptism, marriage, burial registers for Cannstatt, Calw, Untersontheim, Pflummern, Klosterreichenbach, etc.) but almost all are browse-only or low-percent indexed — Archion (subscription) is the most complete single online destination for original Württemberg Lutheran church-book images across this period.
- **Language:** German (Protestant parish records in Württemberg were kept in German, not Latin, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records); be prepared for old German (Kurrent) handwriting.

### Census records
- **National/state census:** This survey found no Württemberg-specific census collection; the Germany_Census wiki page lists documented census programs only for Mecklenburg-Schwerin, Prussian Saxony, Schleswig-Holstein (under Danish rule), and Lübeck — none for Württemberg — so a Württemberg census for 1780-1830 is not confirmed by this survey (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Census).

- **Access:** Not applicable — no collection identified.

### Probate and court records

Here is the locality guide for **Kolonica, Slovakia** (saved as **loc_001**):

---

## Kolonica, Slovakia — Locality Guide, 1700s–1890s

**Jurisdictional Context**

Kolonica is a small village in what is now **Snina district, Slovakia**. For the entire period you're researching (1700s–1918), it was part of **Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary**. Older records are therefore filed under Hungarian county/kingdom archives, not Slovak ones.

---

## Church Records — What Was Found

| Record Type | Date Range | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Greek Catholic parish register (baptisms, marriages, deaths) | **1824–1833** and **1890–1924** | Written in Latin and Hungarian |

**Key findings:**
- The confirmed Greek Catholic parish register **does not reach back into the 1700s**. It begins in 1824, then has an apparent gap, resuming in 1890.
- The original registers were **microfilmed from an archive in Levoča, Slovakia**.
- One of the two source microfilms is **not viewable online** on FamilySearch; the other is part of FamilySearch's Slovak church-book collection.
- **No earlier volumes** (pre-1824) or gap-filling volumes (1834–1889) were located in this search.

---

## Coverage Gaps

- **1700s–1823:** No church records were located for this period. It's unknown whether earlier volumes exist but are unindexed/unfilmed, or were lost.
- **1834–1889:** An apparent gap in the surviving register. It is unconfirmed whether volumes for these years exist elsewhere.
- FamilySearch Wiki pages for this place and for Slovakia could not be fully retrieved during this search, so civil registration start dates and courthouse-held records remain unconfirmed.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Search the available parish register** for 1824–1833 and 1890–1924 on FamilySearch (Slovak church-book collection).
2. **Check the non-viewable microfilm** — it may require ordering through a FamilySearch affiliate library.
3. **Contact the Levoča archive directly** (Štátny archív v Prešove, pracovisko Levoča) to ask about pre-1824 and 1834–1889 volumes.
4. **Re-visit the FamilySearch Wiki** pages for Kolonica and Zemplén County directly for civil registration and courthouse records guidance.
5. Consider whether **Roman Catholic or Reformed church records** from neighboring parishes may cover Kolonica ancestors not in the Greek Catholic registers.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** 1761
- **Location:** Far western Massachusetts, bordering New York to the west and Vermont to the north — a cross-border research situation that matters significantly (see Research Tips below)
- **State-level vital registration:** Did not begin in Massachusetts until **1841** (Boston excluded until 1850); for 1820–1840, the authoritative source is the **town clerk's register**, not a state record

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- **Town clerk registers** are the primary source for 1820–1850
- A digitized volume — "Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850" — covers Berkshire County (FamilySearch image group **004500891**, 512 images)
- ⚠️ **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image by image
- **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (FamilySearch collection **2061550**) is the statewide indexed alternative — start here first
- Marriage intentions were commonly recorded in the **bride's hometown**, possibly also the groom's and their town of residence — check all three

### Church Records
- A Congregational church record volume for **Pittsfield, 1791–1850** was confirmed (FamilySearch image group **004500892**, 274 images)
- ⚠️ Also **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — browse only
- **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (FamilySearch collection **1921657**) covers this period as a statewide indexed collection
- Church registers often substitute for or supplement incomplete civil registrations in this era

### Census Records
- Federal censuses for **1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850** fall within your period
- Access via FamilySearch and Ancestry.com

### Probate Records
- **Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991** (FamilySearch collection **1678901**) covers your period
- Originals held at Berkshire County Probate Court
- Useful for identifying heirs, guardians, and family structure when vital records are sparse

### Naturalization / Passenger Records
- **Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906** (FamilySearch collection **1459213**)
- **Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891** (FamilySearch collection **1784312**) — relevant only if the family immigrated

### Military Records
- Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) — service and pension records
- NARA (https://www.archives.gov) — originals

### Cemetery Records
- Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com)

### Newspapers
- Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) — obituaries and marriage notices

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Statewide indexed vital, church, probate, naturalization collections; browse-only image groups 004500891 & 004500892 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. federal census records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service & pension records | Subscription |
| NARA | Federal originals (passenger lists, military, naturalization) | Free/on-site |
| Town clerk's office | Original 1820–1850 vital record books | Physical |

---

## Records NOT Yet Online (or Only Browse-Only)
- The two Berkshire County-specific volumes (**004500891** and **004500892**) are digitized images but have **no name index** — you must flip through them page by page
- Land records, tax lists, and detailed county court records were **not located in any online index** in this survey — treat them as physical/microfilm until a dedicated search is run

---

## ⚠️ Critical Research Tip: Cross-Border Records
Because the family's town sits close to both the **New York and Vermont state lines**, their records may just as easily appear in a neighboring town or county across those lines. Cross-border church attendance, marriage, and residence were common in this region. **Do not skip searches in adjacent New York and Vermont jurisdictions.**

---

## Recommended Search Order
1. **FamilySearch statewide indexed collections first** (free, name-searchable):
   - Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (collection 2061550)
   - Church Records 1630–1920 (collection 1921657)
   - Probate Records 1635–1991 (collection 1678901)
2. **Browse the two Berkshire-specific image groups** page by page:
   - Town clerk records: image group 004500891
   - Pittsfield Congregational church records: image group 004500892
3. **Census records** (Ancestry or FamilySearch) for 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850
4. **Cross-border searches** in adjacent New York and Vermont towns
5. **Supplementary sources**: Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Jalisco became the 9th state of Mexico on 23 December 1823 (place_search: "Jalisco, Mexico", dateRange +1823/; Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Jalisco,_Mexico_Genealogy)
- **Capital/administrative center:** Guadalajara
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United Mexican States (national level governs civil registration law)
- **Population during period:** Jalisco ~983,500 (1882) to ~1,208,900 (1910), per populstat estimates (http://populstat.info/Americas/mexicop.htm); national population rose from ~10.26 million (1880) to ~14.57 million (1920) (Gapminder, https://www.gapminder.org/data/documentation/gd003/)
- **Indigenous populations:** two significant groups, the Huichol and the Nahua, plus a minority Otomí population that migrated north from the Spanish conquest era (Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Jalisco,_Mexico_Genealogy)
- **Religious denominations:** overwhelmingly Roman Catholic; the Archdiocese of Guadalajara is the central ecclesiastical authority for the state (Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy; Mexico Getting Started, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Getting_Started)
- **Key historical events affecting records:** the 1859 civil registration law (Benito Juárez, Veracruz) met early resistance and was only "vigorously enforced" after the republic was restored in 1867; the separation of church and state was formalized in the 1917 constitution, after which civil (not just church) marriage was required for legal recognition (Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration)

## Boundary changes
- This survey found no record of a boundary change affecting Jalisco as a state during 1880-1920; place_search_all returned only the single standing state-level jurisdiction "Jalisco, Mexico" (date range +1823/) for this name within Mexico.
- Within the state, individual municipios could be renamed (e.g., the catalog notes that Atemajac de las Tablas was renamed Atemajac de Brizuela on 25 April 1903 by decree 997 — koha:666457) — a reminder that municipio-level names in records from this period may not match a modern map, even though the state boundary itself did not change.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** national civil registration law took effect 28 July 1859; enforcement was weak until the republic was restored in 1867 (Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration). Registration is implemented and archived at the municipio level in Jalisco.
- **What exists:** Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration, 1857-2000 (collection 1918187, FamilySearch, index & images, 28,607,850 persons) covers births, marriages, and deaths for the 1880-1920 target window.
- **Where held:** municipio civil registry offices created the records; FamilySearch holds the digitized index & images online. Ancestry also lists separate Jalisco birth (1857-1948, collection 60400), marriage (1861-1961, collection 60436), and death (1856-1987, collection 60464) indexes ($).
- **Gaps:** most individual volume_search coverage rows for this period and place are 0% record-searchable images in Spanish, meaning many years/municipios must be browsed page by page, not searched by name.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** for events before 1867 (or where registration lagged), use the parallel Catholic Church baptism/marriage/burial series below.

### Church records
- **Denomination present:** Roman Catholic (Archdiocese of Guadalajara), per Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Location:** Barony of Lower Dunluce (and partly Carey), poor law union of Coleraine, County Antrim, Ulster province
- **Post towns:** Bushmills; part of Dunserverick
- **From 1922:** Northern Ireland, United Kingdom — records custody falls primarily under PRONI
- **Denominations present:** Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Covenanters, Wesleyan Methodist, Roman Catholic (Coleraine district)

---

## Civil Registration
Government registration of births and deaths began only in **1864**; Protestant marriages from **1845**, all marriages from **1864**. For the bulk of the 1780–1870 target window there are **no civil vital records** — church registers are the essential source.

---

## Church Records

### What Has Been Found Online (FamilySearch)
| Record Set | Date Range | Image Group | Searchability |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ballylinny/Billy christenings | 1837–1868 | 007907410_008_M9VF-SK5 | Full-text, 0% name-indexed |
| Ballylinny/Billy marriages | 1837–1864 | 007765074_009_M9VX-Q7W | Full-text, 0% name-indexed |
| Deffrick National School Girls | 1867–1933 | 008682995_005_M94W-68Y | Browse only, 0% indexed |

No Church of Ireland, Catholic, or pre-1837 Presbyterian registers for Billy parish surfaced in FamilySearch's catalog, collections, or volume searches — leaving **c. 1780–1836 uncovered online** for all denominations.

### Gap-Closing Repositories & Online Indexes

**Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)**
- Holds county-wide church register microfilm and originals for all denominations
- Publishes a parish-by-parish *Guide to Church Records*
- **Address:** 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast BT3 9HQ
- **Email:** proni@communities-ni.gov.uk | **Tel:** 028 9053 4800
- **Guide (PDF):** https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf
- **Digitised church records list:** https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni

**RCB Library (Church of Ireland Representative Church Body Library)**
- Holds/indexes Church of Ireland parish registers; publishes List of Parish Registers
- **Address:** Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735
- **Tel:** +353 (0)1 492 3979 | **Email:** library@ireland.anglican.org
- **Parish Registers list (PDF):** https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf

**RootsIreland (Ulster Historical Foundation)**
- Name-level index for many Ulster parish registers, including Antrim
- **URL:** https://www.rootsireland.ie/ *(subscription)*

**FindMyPast**
- Ireland Non-Conformist Births & Baptisms, Marriages, Burials, and Congregational Records indexes — especially valuable for Presbyterian and Methodist registers
- Betham, Crossle & Thrift Genealogical Abstracts (substitutes for registers lost in the 1922 Public Record Office of Ireland fire)
- **URL:** https://www.findmypast.com/ *(subscription)*

**National Library of Ireland — Catholic Parish Registers**
- Free online index; covers many Catholic registers to 1880
- **URL:** https://registers.nli.ie/

**Ancestry**
- Ireland Catholic Parish Registers 1655–1915
- Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds Indexes 1623–1866
- Abstracts of Wills & Marriages 1620–1923
- **URL:** https://www.ancestry.com/ *(subscription)*

---

## Census Substitutes (Pre-1864 vital-record gap)
Pre-1901 Irish census returns were largely destroyed. Use these in their place:

| Record | Coverage | FamilySearch Volume |
|---|---|---|
| Tithe Applotment Books | 1820s | Available via FamilySearch |
| Griffith's Valuation | 1840s–1870s | VAL 12B/1/7B, 1867–1881 (browse-only) |

---

## Known Record Losses
- Two-thirds of Church of Ireland parish registers nationwide were destroyed in the **1922 PRO Dublin fire**. Whether Billy parish's Church of Ireland registers were among the losses has not been confirmed; the Betham/Crossle/Thrift abstracts at FindMyPast may compensate.

---

## Research Strategy
1. **Identify the family's denomination first** — this determines which registers to target. Presbyterian and Church of Ireland families together made up c. 60% of the 1861 Antrim population; Catholics c. 40%.
2. **Search the FamilySearch digitized volumes** (christenings 1837–1868 and marriages 1837–1864) first — free and full-text searchable even without a name index.
3. **For anything pre-1837 or for Catholic/Church of Ireland registers**, contact PRONI in Belfast and check the RCB Library; also try RootsIreland and FindMyPast name-level indexes.
4. **Catholic parishes did not follow civil-parish boundaries** — search the Coleraine Catholic district records and neighbouring parishes if Billy results are thin.
5. **Use Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation** as census substitutes for the entire 1780–1870 window.
6. **Check Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) for memorial inscriptions that can substitute for missing burial registers.

# Locality Guide: Christ Church, Philadelphia — Marriage Register (1734)

## The Short Answer

The original 1734 marriage register belongs to **Christ Church, Philadelphia itself** — not to a government archive or the diocese. Per FamilySearch's Pennsylvania Church Records guidance, original registers stay with active parishes; because Christ Church has never closed, the Diocese of Pennsylvania does not hold its pre-closure records. **No digitized image of the original register was found on FamilySearch or in the FamilySearch Catalog during this survey.**

---

## Why There Is No Civil/Government Record
Pennsylvania did not begin statewide civil registration of marriages until **1913**. A 1734 marriage long predates any government-held original — the church register is the only primary source.

---

## Where to Find the Original

| Custodian | What They Hold | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Christ Church, Philadelphia** (the parish itself) | The original colonial registers, including the 1734 marriage book, presumed to remain in parish custody | **Contact the church directly** to arrange viewing or obtain a copy |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | *Abstracts* (summaries) taken from various Pennsylvania church records — **not the original register** | Useful for locating the entry; not a substitute for the original |

---

## Online Derivative Sources (Not Originals)

These collections are free on FamilySearch and indexed, so you can confirm the marriage entry quickly before contacting the parish — but they are compiled indexes or abstracts, not page images of the 1734 register:

- **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (FamilySearch collection id 1571957; 624,090 people)
- **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (FamilySearch collection id 1502909; 397,530 people)
- **Pennsylvania, HSP, Marriages (1512–1989)** — the Historical Society of Pennsylvania's abstract set, which the FamilySearch Wiki explicitly describes as *derivative*, not an image of the original

---

## What Was Not Found

A `catalog_search` for "Christ Church marriages" at Philadelphia returned **zero hits** — meaning no digitized image volume of that register has been catalogued on FamilySearch. This is a cataloguing gap, not proof the register was lost. No source in this survey reported it destroyed or transferred elsewhere.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Search the online indexes first** (the two FamilySearch collections above) to confirm the exact entry and parties — free and fast.
2. **Contact Christ Church, Philadelphia directly** to ask about access to the original 1734 marriage register. Since the church is active, that is the authoritative custodian per FamilySearch Wiki guidance.
3. As a fallback, ask the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** whether it holds any additional Christ Church materials beyond its abstract collection.
4. Try a broader FamilySearch Catalog search under "Christ Church" (without the "marriages" filter) in case the register is catalogued under a different title.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Mississippi Territory (c. 1798–1819)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Present-day Alabama was part of the **Mississippi Territory** from 1798 to 1817, then the separate **Alabama Territory** from 1817 until statehood in 1819. So an ancestor "in the Alabama region around 1800" was legally in the Mississippi Territory — Alabama did not yet exist. Before U.S. control, the Mobile Bay area passed through French (1702–1763), British (1763–1780), and Spanish (1780–1813) hands.

---

## Available Record Types

### Territorial Census Records
Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama.
- **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery — not shown to be online by this survey; likely physical access only.

### Federal Census Overlap
FamilySearch's **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (collection 2016756, ~287,000 persons) begins in 1810 and covers the late territorial period.

### Church Records
- Spanish-era Mobile District church registers are in Spanish and held at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress**.
- FamilySearch's **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** (collection id 1986396, ~157,000 persons) begins at 1803 and overlaps the target window.

### Land Records
- Earliest records are Spanish and British colonial land grants in the Mobile area.
- A digitized but **unindexed, browse-only** FamilySearch volume (image group 004512889, 214 images, 0% indexed) covers **"Territorial Court and Land Records, 1808–1819"** — directly in the target window, but must be browsed page by page.

### Probate / Court Records
- FamilySearch **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (collection 1537764, ~438,000 persons) begins in 1809.
- A second browse-only volume (image group 004512890, 96 images, 0% indexed) covers **"Washington County Deed and Probate Records, 1803–1820"** — Washington District was an early Mississippi Territory subdivision covering much of present western Alabama.

### Marriage Records
- FamilySearch **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** (collection 1598408, ~1.2 million persons) begins in 1809.

### Military Records
- For conflicts touching the period (War of 1812, Creek War 1813–1814), service and pension records would be held at **NARA** (archives.gov); no territorial-specific collection was confirmed.

### Colonial-Era Records
- **French (1702–1763):** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm copies at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Spanish (1780–1813):** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at the Library of Congress.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History, Montgomery** | Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810 | Physical / contact repository |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Church (1803+), probate (1809+), marriage (1809+), census substitute (1810+), two browse-only territorial volumes | Free online |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Federal land, military, naturalization records | Online & physical |
| **Library of Congress** | Copies of Spanish Mobile District church/land records | Physical / some digitized |
| **Archivo General de Indias (Seville)** | Spanish colonial originals for Mobile District | Physical |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence)** | French colonial records, Mobile area 1702–1763 | Physical |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Microfilm of French colonial records | Physical |

---

## Records NOT Online (as of this survey)
- Territorial censuses (1801–1810) at ADAH
- Both FamilySearch digitized territorial volumes are **0% indexed** — image browsing only, no name search
- Spanish, British, and French colonial originals in Seville and Aix-en-Provence

---

## Research Tips

1. **Use the right jurisdiction name.** Records from this era are filed under "Mississippi Territory" (and after 1817, "Alabama Territory"), not "Alabama." A search limited to the modern state name will miss territorial-period records.

2. **Start online, then go physical.** Begin with the indexed FamilySearch collections (probate 1809+, church 1803+, census 1810+); then browse the two unindexed territorial volumes page by page; then contact ADAH for the 1801–1810 territorial censuses.

3. **Washington County is key.** Washington District/County was one of the earliest Mississippi Territory subdivisions and covered much of present western Alabama — worth checking even if your ancestor's later-known Alabama county didn't yet exist in 1800.

4. **Check the colonial layer if Mobile area.** If your ancestor was in or near Mobile Bay, there may be Spanish-era church baptism/marriage/burial records surviving in Seville or at the Library of Congress.

5. **Identify the specific location.** Once you can pin down a more precise district, settlement, or county (even approximate), a focused research plan can target the territorial censuses, land entries, or church registers that actually cover that ground.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Spanish Colonial Period, c. 1763–1800)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The modern state of Arkansas did not exist in this period. The area was held by **France** (as part of La Louisiane), passed to **Spain** under the 1763 Treaty of Paris, then secretly retroceded to France in 1800, before the United States acquired it via the **1803 Louisiana Purchase**. Arkansas was not admitted as a U.S. state until 1836.

**Administrative center:** **Arkansas Post**, founded by the French in 1686, served as the civil and military hub for the district under Spanish administration.

**Parent jurisdiction:** Spanish Louisiana (Luisiana), 1763–1800, administered from New Orleans.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary genealogical source)*
- **What:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials recorded by French Catholic missionaries at Arkansas Post.
- **Language:** Spanish (colonial script and terminology — *bautismo, matrimonio, entierro*).
- **Where held:**
  - **FamilySearch** has digitized one volume: Image Group **008814402**, *"Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial),"* Arkansas Post, 1763–1800 — 64 images, **browse-only** (no name index, not full-text searchable). Free access.
  - **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** holds the originals or is custodian.
  - **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock) holds transcribed copies.

### Colonial Administrative Records (Census, Land, Military)
- **Padrones (colonial censuses):** Spanish colonial censuses were kept at Arkansas Post. None are confirmed online or indexed.
- **Land concessions:** Spanish authorities granted colonial land concessions at Arkansas Post. These are not digitized.
- **Military post records:** Garrison rolls and correspondence exist but are not separately itemized online.
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain); **Library of Congress** microfilm.

### What Does NOT Apply to This Period
- **U.S. federal or territorial census:** The first U.S. census that could cover this area is 1810, after the Louisiana Purchase.
- **State vital records or civil registration:** Arkansas statehood was 1836; no U.S. civil registration applied here before 1800.
- **Standard U.S. county records:** None existed yet.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Digitized sacramental register (008814402), 1763–1800, browse-only, Spanish | Free online |
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock) | Transcribed church registers; colonial records incl. land concessions | Visit or write |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original sacramental registers from Arkansas Post | Visit or diocesan archive |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana/Arkansas district | Visit or Spanish national archive |
| **Library of Congress** | Microfilm of Spanish colonial records | Microfilm services |

---

## Records NOT Online

Spanish colonial land concessions, padrones, and military post administrative records are **not available in any online database** found by this survey — they exist only at the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias, and on Library of Congress microfilm.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with FamilySearch image group 008814402** — it is free and already online. It must be browsed page-by-page in Spanish, but it covers the full 1763–1800 period.
2. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission** — their transcribed copies may be easier to search than the Spanish-language originals.
3. **For land, census, or administrative records**, contact the Archivo General de Indias or use Library of Congress microfilm.
4. **Brush up on Spanish colonial terminology** — *padrón* (census), *bautismo* (baptism), *matrimonio* (marriage), *entierro* (burial).
5. **Broaden your search to Spanish Louisiana** — settlers moving along the Mississippi/Arkansas Rivers may also appear in broader Spanish Louisiana records centered on New Orleans.
6. The Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias have their own online catalogs; FamilySearch's general catalog returned no hits for Arkansas in this period (a cataloguing gap, not evidence records don't exist).

---

**Bottom line:** The one genealogically useful record series confirmed online for this period is the **Spanish-language Catholic church register at Arkansas Post** (FamilySearch, browse-only). Related land, census, and administrative records survive on paper at the Arkansas History Commission, the Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, Spain's Archivo General de Indias, and on Library of Congress microfilm. Modern Arkansas county and state records start decades too late to help for pre-1800 research.

This is a temporal, not geographic, succession: the same territory around Arkansas Post was held in turn by France (to 1763), Spain (1763–1800), France again (1800–1803), then the United States.
