# Locality Guide: Ohio (pre-1790, Northwest Territory period)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Ohio did not exist as a jurisdiction in 1790. The area was governed by the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Washington County was the first county organized within the territory (1788), followed by Hamilton County (1790).

---

## Boundary Changes

This was a **geographic and administrative organization period**, not a simple predecessor-successor split. The Northwest Territory was progressively subdivided into counties as settlement advanced. Which county held jurisdiction over a 1790 event depends on **exactly where in the territory it occurred**, and boundaries shifted repeatedly before Ohio achieved statehood in 1803.

> **Key tip:** Records for this period will be found under whatever county then held that specific territory — not under "Ohio" as a state. Researchers must identify the county boundary in force at the time of the event, not assume today's county lines.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- No statewide civil vital-registration system existed yet.
- **Church records and county court/land records** are the primary alternatives.
- **"Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013"** (FamilySearch collection id 1803785, ~3M persons) overlaps 1790 and is held at the county level.

### Church Records
- **"Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950"** (FamilySearch collection id 2246917, ~678K persons) overlaps the 1790 period.
- Specific denominations active in the territory in 1790 were not confirmed by this survey.

### Census Records
- The first U.S. federal census was 1790, but the Northwest Territory was largely outside settled enumeration districts at that date — no 1790 federal census collection specific to this territory was found.
- **Substitute:** Tax records (see below) are the best-confirmed substitute for missing 1790s census coverage.

### Probate and Court Records
- Early court and land records are held at the **Ohio History Connection, Columbus** (per the FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio, United States Genealogy").
- No digitized probate collection for this period surfaced in this survey.

### Land Records
Two distinct land-distribution systems operated side by side:

| System | Location | Records Held At |
|--------|-----------|-----------------|
| Virginia Military District | Between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers (bounty land for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans; metes-and-bounds survey) | Virginia State Library |
| Connecticut Western Reserve | Northeastern Ohio (grid survey system) | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |

- **"Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840"** (FamilySearch collection id 1542187) is name-indexed.
- A browse-only volume, image group **005112233** (51 images, 0% indexed) covers "Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799" — must be browsed image by image.

### Tax Records
- **"Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850"** (FamilySearch collection id 1987542) starts just after 1790.
- A partially-indexed browse volume, image group **005112240** (73 images, 12% indexed) covers "County Tax Records, 1799–1803" for Washington County — the best near-period substitute for missing census coverage.

### Military Records
- Relevant primarily for Virginia Military District bounty-land claims (post-Revolutionary War context).
- Likely held at NARA/Virginia State Library; not independently confirmed by a tool result in this survey.

### Cemetery, Newspaper, Immigration Records
- No collections for this place and period were returned by this survey. Early frontier settlement makes local newspapers from 1790 unlikely.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories (Free via FamilySearch)
| Collection | ID | Persons | Period |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ohio, County Marriages | 1803785 | ~3,047,000 | 1789–2013 |
| Ohio, Church Records | 2246917 | ~678,000 | 1787–1950 |
| Ohio, Land Records | 1787–1840 | 1542187 | ~234,000 |
| Ohio, Tax Records | 1800–1850 | 1987542 | ~345,000 |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Early territorial court and land records |
| Virginia State Library | Virginia Military District land warrants |
| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records |

---

## Known Record Losses
This survey found no tool result stating that any specific record set for this place and period was destroyed. The near-total absence of name-indexed or full-text material in the two digitized volumes (0% and 12% indexed) reflects a **digitization gap, not record loss** — treat it accordingly.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search under the right jurisdiction.** Because Ohio didn't exist in 1790, search under "Northwest Territory" and the specific organized county (Washington County from 1788; Hamilton County from 1790) for the location at that date.
2. **Start with indexed FamilySearch collections** — "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" (id 2246917) and "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (id 1542187) — before turning to the browse-only volumes.
3. **Browse-only volumes** (image groups 005112233 and 005112240) must be gone through image by image — neither is name-searchable.
4. **Route land-grant research by district:** Virginia Military District claims → Virginia State Library; Connecticut Western Reserve claims → Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
5. **Tax and land/court records are your best substitutes** for the absence of vital registration and census coverage in the 1790s — focus on the Ohio History Connection in Columbus.
6. **Pin down the exact location** of your ancestor's event first, since that location — not modern Ohio county lines — determines which county's records to search.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush era)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state in 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely. Before that it was Mexican, then Spanish colonial, territory.
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855, drawing roughly 300,000 migrants.
- **Key event:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, Coloma, January 24, 1848; statehood 1850.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **County Births, 1850–1919** — FamilySearch collection id 2017276 (789,456 persons indexed), held originally at county recorder offices.
- **County Marriages, 1850–1952** — FamilySearch collection id 1452832 (1,135,780 persons indexed).
- **Gap:** No statewide *death* record collection for this period was found in this survey.

### Church Records
- **California, Mission Records, 1769–1850** — FamilySearch collection id 1804372 (98,765 persons indexed). Catholic mission baptisms, marriages, and burials; records are in Spanish.
- No Protestant or other denominational register collection for 1848–1860 was confirmed in this survey.

### Census Records
- **1850 Federal Census** — the first taken in California, but some county returns are **missing/destroyed**; treat as incomplete.
- **California State Census, 1850–1852** — digitized volume (image group 006601001, 522 images, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable). Best substitute where the federal census is missing.

### Probate and Court Records
- Not confirmed by any place-specific tool result in this survey; original holdings would be at county courthouses or the California State Archives.

### Land & Mining Claim Records
- A digitized volume covering **San Francisco Mining Claim Registers, 1849–1855** (image group 006601002, 340 images) exists but is **0% indexed** — browse-only.
- Federal land patents run through the BLM General Land Office, but no GLO-specific California confirmation was returned in this survey.

### Military Records
- Not addressed by any California-specific tool result in this survey; U.S. service records, pensions, and draft registrations are held at NARA generally.

### Immigration / Port Records
- **San Francisco ship passenger manifests** — National Archives, San Bruno (the principal port of entry for Gold Rush arrivals by sea).
- **Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858** — digitized volume (image group 006601003, 298 images), **0% indexed, not full-text searchable** — browse-only.
- **Overland migrants:** Left trail diaries and journals rather than manifests; held as manuscript material at the Bancroft Library and California State Library — not in any online database.

### Voter Registration (Post-period context)
- **California, Great Registers, 1866–1910** — FamilySearch collection id 1923340 (1,345,678 persons). Begins after the target window, but useful for tracing a Gold Rush migrant's later settled life.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Coverage |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | County births/marriages; mission records; state census; mining claim & port arrival browse volumes; Great Registers (post-1866) |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census |
| **Fold3** | Military records |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Passenger manifests, military/pension records |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records (generic; no county-specific coverage confirmed) |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers (generic; no title/date range confirmed for this period) |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **National Archives, San Bruno** | San Francisco ship passenger manifests |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush–era manuscript collections (diaries, journals) |
| **California State Library** | Gold Rush–era manuscript collections |

---

## Known Record Losses
- The **1850 federal census** for California is partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. The 1850–1852 state census is the best substitute.
- Mining claim and port arrival registers are digitized but **unsearchable by name** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — must be browsed page by page.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the California State Census, 1850–1852** (FamilySearch image group 006601001) — 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable; fastest way to locate a named migrant.
2. Next check **County Births and County Marriages** (FamilySearch ids 2017276 and 1452832) — both indexed.
3. For sea arrivals, check **San Francisco ship passenger manifests** at the National Archives, San Bruno, or browse the **Port Arrival Registers** (image group 006601003) on FamilySearch.
4. For mining activity, browse the **Mining Claim Registers** (image group 006601002) on FamilySearch — no index, so narrow to county and date range first.
5. For overland migrants who left no port record, look for **trail diaries and journals** at the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) or the California State Library — manuscript-only, not online.
6. After the 1860s, trace a settler further using the **Great Registers, 1866–1910** (collection id 1923340).
7. **Narrow to a county** before searching: many Gold Rush–era records are county-level, and county formation dates matter — a mining camp may have belonged to a different county in 1852 than in 1858.

---

*Survey scope: California statewide, 1848–1860. Many records from this period are unindexed, incompletely digitized, or manuscript-only. Combining an indexed database search with physical archive visits is likely necessary for a thorough investigation.*

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a U.S. state in 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely (per place_search, dateRange "+1850/"; Wikipedia, "California Gold Rush," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Gold_Rush). Before that it was Mexican, then Spanish colonial, territory.
- **Population during period:** This survey's population-data call returned no figures for California for 1848–1860 — not confirmed by this survey.
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855, drawing roughly 300,000 migrants per the Wikipedia summary above.
- **Ethnic composition:** The migrant population was transient and predominantly male, drawn from diverse domestic and foreign origins (Wikipedia, as above).
- **Religious denominations:** Franciscan missions operated 1769–1834 and are documented in mission registers (FamilySearch Wiki, "California Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records).
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, Coloma, January 24, 1848; statehood 1850 (Wikipedia, as above).

## Boundary changes
California entered the Union in 1850 as a state, not a territory, so there was no intervening territorial record series to connect — this survey found no boundary changes affecting record jurisdiction during 1848–1860. Many of today's counties were created or subdivided during the Gold Rush years as mining camps grew into towns, so a researcher should check county formation dates for any specific camp or town of interest before assuming which county recorder held an 1850s record.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not confirmed by this survey for the state level; the "California, County Births, 1850-1919" and "California, County Marriages, 1850-1952" collections (collections_search, ids 2017276 and 1452832) begin in 1850 and are held at the county level.
- **What exists:** County-level birth records from 1850 (789,456 persons indexed, collection 2017276) and county marriage records from 1850 (1,135,780 persons indexed, collection 1452832).
- **Where held:** County recorder offices originally; indexed on FamilySearch as above.
- **Gaps:** No statewide death-record collection for this period was returned by collections_search — a coverage gap, not evidence of absence.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Franciscan mission registers, 1769–1850 (see Church records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic missions, 1769–1834 (FamilySearch Wiki, "California Genealogy," as above). No other denomination's founding dates were returned by this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials in the mission registers.
- **Where held:** "California, Mission Records, 1769-1850" is indexed on FamilySearch, 98,765 persons (collection 1804372).

- **Language:** Mission records are in Spanish; this survey did not retrieve an explicit statement to that effect from a tool result, so treat it as expected but unconfirmed here, and read originals accordingly.

### Census records

- **State census:** A California State Census, 1850–1852, exists as a digitized volume (image group 006601001, 522 images, 88% name-indexed, full-text searchable) — indexed + images.
- **Other enumerations:** No mortality schedule or tax-list enumeration specific to California for this period was returned by this survey.
- **Access:** The state census volume above is both name-indexed and full-text searchable; the 1850 federal census's destroyed portions are a known loss (see below).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Not detailed by any tool result for this place and period — this survey did not confirm specific probate holdings.
- **Where held:** Generically, county courthouses or state archives, per the fallback FamilySearch Wiki research-guide page read in this survey (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide) — but that page is a generic template, not California-specific, so treat this as general guidance only.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Mining claim registers were kept locally; a digitized volume covering San Francisco, 1849–1855 (image group 006601002, 340 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable) is browse-only.
- **Types:** Mining claims; land grants/patents at the federal level would run through the BLM General Land Office per the generic FamilySearch Wiki page, but no GLO-specific confirmation for California was returned.
- **Where held:** Original mining claim registers held locally (county/district recorders); FamilySearch's digitized copy (above) must be browsed image by image, with no name index.

### Military records
Not addressed by any place-specific tool result for this period; the FamilySearch Wiki pages read in this survey returned only generic U.S. boilerplate (service records, pensions, and draft registrations at NARA) rather than California-specific detail.

### Cemetery records
No California-specific cemetery collection was returned by this survey. Find A Grave is available generically (external_links_search, https://www.findagrave.com/) but with no county-specific coverage confirmed here.

### Newspaper records
No California Gold Rush-era newspaper collection or title was returned by this survey. Newspapers.com is listed generically (external_links_search, https://www.newspapers.com/) with no date range or title confirmed for this place and period.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests at San Francisco, held at the National Archives, San Bruno (FamilySearch Wiki, "California Genealogy," as above). A digitized volume labeled "Port Arrival Registers," Sacramento, 1849–1858, 298 images, 0% indexed and not full-text searchable (image group 006601003), is browse-only.

Not addressed by any place-specific tool result in this survey.

"California, Great Registers, 1866-1910" (collections_search, id 1923340, 1,345,678 persons) is a voter-registration series, but it begins in 1866 — after this 1848–1860 target window — so it is background context only, useful for tracing a Gold Rush migrant's later settled life, not the migration itself.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | California, County Births 1850-1919 (id 2017276); California, County Marriages 1850-1952 (id 1452832); California, Mission Records 1769-1850 (id 1804372); California, Great Registers 1866-1910 (id 1923340); digitized volumes for State Census 1850-1852, Mining Claim Registers 1849-1855, Port Arrival Registers 1849-1858 | Civil vital records, mission-era church records, voter rolls (post-1866) | Free |

| California State Library | Gold Rush-era manuscript collections | In person / archive request |

(All three per FamilySearch Wiki, "California Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records.)

## Records NOT online
Mining claim registers and port arrival registers are digitized but exist only as browse-only image sets with no name index (0% searchable, not full-text searchable) — they must be paged through image by image. Overland trail diaries and journals are manuscript material at the Bancroft Library and California State Library, not in any online database. County probate, tax, and newspaper holdings for this period were not located online by this survey and should be assumed physical-only until checked directly with the county or a library.

## Known record losses
The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed; some county returns are missing (FamilySearch Wiki, "California Genealogy," as above). This loss is stated specifically for the 1850 federal census returns, not for the state census or other record types in this guide. The California State Census of 1850–1852 (image group 006601001) is a partial substitute where the federal count is missing.

- **Search order:** Start with the California State Census, 1850-1852 (image group 006601001) — it is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable, so it is the fastest way to locate a named migrant. Then browse the Mining Claim Registers (006601002) and Port Arrival Registers (006601003) image by image, since neither is indexed.
- Where the 1850 federal census is missing for a county, substitute the 1850–1852 state census described above (FamilySearch Wiki, "California Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records).
- For an ancestor who arrived before 1850 and left no mission or civil record, look for overland trail diaries and journals at the Bancroft Library or California State Library — these are manuscript, not database, sources (same page).
- If a migrant is not found in the 1866+ Great Registers, that collection starts after this period and is not evidence the person did not later settle in California — check it only for post-1866 traces.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's general research-guide pages returned only generic U.S. boilerplate content in this survey rather than California-specific detail for vital records start dates, probate, military, or tax records; treat those topics as unconfirmed and consult the Wiki directly for California-specific articles beyond "California Genealogy."
- The FamilySearch Catalog search for California returned zero hits in this survey — a cataloguing gap, not evidence that no microfilm or manuscript holdings exist; a narrower catalog search by county or surname may surface results this broad query did not.

This survey looked at California statewide for the 1848 to 1860 Gold Rush years and found that the main places to search are FamilySearch's online collections of county birth and marriage records, a state census taken in 1850-1852, and digitized but unsearchable mining-claim and port-arrival registers that must be read page by page; manuscript diaries and letters from people who traveled overland are kept only on paper at the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley and the California State Library, and the 1850 federal census has some county returns missing. The biggest warnings are that many records from this chaotic, fast-growing period are either not indexed by name, not digitized at all, or simply did not survive, so expect to combine an indexed record with browsing an image set or visiting an archive in person. The next step would be to narrow the search to a specific county, mining camp, or family surname so a more detailed, targeted record search can be planned.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York — 1700s Colonial Period

## Jurisdiction Overview
New York City was an English colonial city from 1664 (seized from Dutch New Amsterdam, established 1626) and served as capital of the Province of New York. The Dutch-to-English transfer in 1664 is the key dividing point for which colonial administration created which records. The city had a mixed Dutch and English population, with Dutch Reformed, Anglican (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian churches all present.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary substitute for vital registration)*
Church registers served the function of civil birth/marriage/death registration in this era — no civil vital registration existed in the 1700s.

- **Dutch Reformed Church** — oldest continuous series, beginning 1639. A digitized browse-only volume covering **1700–1776** exists on FamilySearch (image group 007733180, 211 images), **but it has 0% name indexing, cannot be text-searched, and is written in Dutch** — you must page through it image by image and read Dutch (or use a translation agent).
- **Anglican (Trinity Church)** and **Presbyterian** registers are mentioned in the FamilySearch Wiki but were **not found as digitized collections** in this survey — treat as physical-only until confirmed otherwise.

### Probate Records
- FamilySearch collection **"New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971"** (id 1542780, ~987,654 people) — spans the full colonial period, name-searchable.
- The **New-York Historical Society** holds published *Abstracts of Wills* proved before the Prerogative Court of New York — a key colonial-era finding aid.
- **Mayor's Court records** (municipal civil/licensing suits) are named in the FamilySearch Wiki but no digitization detail was confirmed.

### Land Records
- FamilySearch collection **"New York, Land Records, 1630–1975"** (id 2078654, ~1,567,890 people) — covers the full colonial period.

### Tax Records *(census substitute)*
No federal census existed before 1790, so colonial tax assessment lists by ward are the nearest substitute.
- FamilySearch collection **"New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804"** (id 1678432) — just after the target period but useful.
- Earlier 1700s ward tax lists are mentioned by the FamilySearch Wiki but no specific digitized collection was confirmed by this survey.

### Church Records (Broad Collection)
- FamilySearch collection **"New York, Church Records, 1640–1940"** (id 1469062, ~2,345,678 people) — name-searchable, free, spans the full colonial period — **start here**.

### Military Records
- Colonial-era militia rolls survive for some years, per the FamilySearch Wiki, but no specific digitized collection was confirmed.
- For the Revolutionary War tail end of this period, **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) holds military service/pension records.

### Newspapers
- The *New York Gazette* is a colonial-era paper that carried marriage notices, death notices, and legal notices.
- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) is the recommended online resource for historical newspaper searching.

### Immigration
- New York City was a major colonial port of entry. Pre-1906 naturalizations appear in any court of record. **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal-level immigration and naturalization records.

### Cemetery Records
- **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the recommended online resource; specific 1700s NYC cemeteries were not confirmed by name in this survey.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1640–1940 (id 1469062); Land Records 1630–1975 (id 2078654); Probate Records 1629–1971 (id 1542780); Tax Rolls 1799–1804 (id 1678432); Dutch Reformed browse-only volume 1700–1776 (image group 007733180) | Free |
| **New-York Historical Society** | Published *Abstracts of Wills*; extensive colonial-era holdings | Physical / vary |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** | Extensive colonial-era collections (mentioned in FamilySearch Wiki) | Physical / vary |
| **NARA** | Federal immigration, military, naturalization | Free |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records | Subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census (post-1790); other records | Subscription |

---

## Records NOT Online (Known Gaps)
- **Anglican (Trinity Church) and Presbyterian registers** — not found as digitized collections; likely physical-only.
- **Colonial militia rolls** for 1700s specifically — not confirmed as a digitized collection.
- **Mayor's Court records** — mentioned by the FamilySearch Wiki but no digitization detail confirmed.

---

## Recommended Search Order
1. **FamilySearch "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940"** (id 1469062) — free, name-indexed, full colonial coverage — *start here*.
2. **FamilySearch "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971"** (id 1542780) — free, name-indexed.
3. **FamilySearch "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975"** (id 2078654) — free, name-indexed.
4. **Dutch Reformed browse-only volume** (image group 007733180) — Dutch language, page-by-page browse only; use if you have a Dutch Reformed ancestor and need baptism/marriage/burial.
5. **New-York Historical Society** *Abstracts of Wills* — for estates proved through the colonial Prerogative Court.
6. **Trinity Church archives** directly — for Anglican registers not confirmed online.

---

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783, Revolutionary War Era)

---

## Jurisdiction Overview
Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies with county-level record-keeping dating to the 1630s. During the Revolutionary War period (1775–1783), Virginia operated as an independent state and contributed more Continental Army troops than any other colony. The decisive Siege of Yorktown was fought on Virginia soil. Virginia's vast western claims at this time included what is now Kentucky and territory beyond the Ohio River — families that "disappear" from Virginia records may have moved into those lands.

---

## Record Types for Military and Wartime Research

### Military Service Records
- **Continental Line service records and muster rolls** — held at the **National Archives (NARA), Record Group 93**
- **Virginia militia records** — held at the **Library of Virginia, Richmond**
- **Virginia State Navy records** — published (specific publication not confirmed by this survey)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (Collection ID 1945678, ~345,678 persons) — indexed, free, matches the exact target period
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678

### Pension & Bounty-Land Warrant Applications (NARA, Record Group 15)
These are often the most genealogically rich source: veterans' depositions frequently include birthplace, family members' names, and migration history. Post-war bounty lands for Virginia veterans were granted in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio**, so a family traced to Ohio may connect back through Virginia warrant and survey records.

A **browse-only bounty-land warrant volume** (Virginia, 1779–1800; image group 005301447, 341 images) exists on FamilySearch but has **no name index and no full-text search** — it must be browsed page by page.

### Tax Records (Census Substitutes)
No federal census existed for 1775–1783, and the 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. **Tax lists are the primary census substitute:**
- **"Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850"** (FamilySearch Collection ID 1456723) — begins within the target window
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723
- A digitized 1782–1799 state tax/enumeration volume (image group 005301449, 87 images) is full-text searchable but not name-indexed

### County Court Records
- **Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795** (image group 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed) — directly within the target period
- **"Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920"** (FamilySearch Collection ID 2134567)
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567
- Wills, estate inventories, administrations, and guardianships were filed at the county court level

### Church/Vital Records
Civil registration did not exist during this period; Anglican/Episcopal parish registers were the primary record of baptisms, marriages, and burials:
- **"Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929"** (FamilySearch Collection ID 1598230)
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230

### Land Records
- **"Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900"** (FamilySearch Collection ID 1734285)
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285

### Cemetery & Newspaper Records
- **Find A Grave** (online): https://www.findagrave.com/
- **Newspapers.com**: https://www.newspapers.com/

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Virginia Military Records 1775–1783 (1945678); Church Records (1598230); Tax Records (1456723); County Court Records (2134567); Land Records (1734285) | Free |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Continental Line service/muster rolls (RG 93); Pension & bounty-land applications (RG 15) | In-person or Fold3/Ancestry online |
| **Library of Virginia, Richmond** | Virginia militia records; state-level wartime records | In-person |
| **Fold3** | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** | Various Virginia collections | Subscription |

---

## Known Record Losses
- The **1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed** (burned with Washington in 1814) — reinforcing the need for 1782 tax lists as a substitute
- The FamilySearch Catalog returned zero hits for a Virginia/Revolutionary War subject search, but this is a cataloguing gap — the records themselves exist at NARA and the Library of Virginia

---

## Recommended Search Order
1. **FamilySearch "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** (ID 1945678) — indexed, free, exact match
2. **Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795** (image group 005301448) — 61% name-indexed
3. **Tax-list substitutes** — "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" and the full-text tax volume
4. **NARA pension and bounty-land files (RG 15)** — rich personal testimony
5. **NARA Continental Line service records (RG 93)** — muster rolls and service details
6. **Bounty-land warrant volume** (image group 005301447) — browse image by image (no index)

---

## Important Notes
- **Continental Line records are federal, not state** — look to NARA, not only Virginia state repositories
- Pension applications are often more genealogically detailed than service records themselves
- If a family disappears from Virginia records after the war, check **Ohio land-warrant and survey records** tied to Virginia Military District bounty-land claims
- The FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia overview pages returned only generic content in this survey; for deeper locality guidance, consult the Library of Virginia or NARA directly

## Boundary changes

- **Where held:** County and parish level.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal parish registers were the primary source of vital-event recording in colonial Virginia; see Church records below.

### Church records

- **Where held:** FamilySearch's **"Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929"** collection (collection ID 1598230, ~1,234,567 person records), which overlaps the target period. https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230

- **Language:** English.

### Census records
No federal census exists for 1775–1783 (the first U.S. census was 1790). For this period, substitutes are essential:
- **Tax lists** are the primary census substitute: FamilySearch's **"Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850"** collection (ID 1456723, ~456,789 persons) begins within the target window. https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships — filed at the county court.
- **Testate or intestate:** Determine from the specific ancestor's probate file; both series exist at county level.
- **Where held:** County court order books. A specific digitized, 61%-name-indexed volume of **Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795** exists: image group 005301448, 158 images. This falls squarely in the target period and county.

### Military records
This is the core record type for the stated research goal:
- **Continental Line service records and muster rolls** — described by the FamilySearch Wiki as held at the National Archives (Record Group 93). https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave is listed among curated external links for Virginia. https://www.findagrave.com/
- **Physical records:** Not confirmed by this survey beyond the online index above.

### Newspaper records
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com is listed among curated external links for Virginia. https://www.newspapers.com/

Not a primary concern for this inland research goal during the war years; this survey found no period-specific immigration record set for Virginia 1775–1783.

### Tax records
See Census records above — tax lists are the chief census substitute for this period, with the **"Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850"** collection and the browse/full-text 1782–1799 tax-list volume (image group 005301449) both falling inside the target window.

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` for Military/Military Pensions/Draft record-type groups, 1775–1783, returned 3 digitized volumes total; all 3 are detailed above — this appears to be the complete matched set for that search, not a partial page.

The browse-only bounty-land-warrant volume (image group 005301447, 341 images, Virginia, 1779–1800) exists digitally but with no name index and no full-text search — it must be browsed image by image. The Virginia State Navy records and the Library of Virginia's militia holdings were not shown by this survey to have any online component.

The FamilySearch Wiki excerpt retrieved in this survey states the 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — relevant as background, since it is why tax lists from the 1780s serve as the standard substitute for population counts in this period. https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands No tool result in this survey addresses the survival or loss of Virginia's colonial-era parish registers or militia muster rolls specifically.

- **Search order:** Start with the free, period-matched **"Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783"** FamilySearch collection (ID 1945678) first, since it is indexed and matches the exact years; then search the **Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795** volume (image group 005301448), which is 61% name-indexed; then the tax-list collections for tax/census substitutes; the bounty-land-warrant volume (005301447) goes last since it must be browsed image by image with no index.

This survey looked at Virginia's record landscape for family history research during the Revolutionary War years, 1775 to 1783, when Virginia sent more soldiers to fight than any other American colony. The most useful materials are military service and pension files held by the National Archives, state militia records kept at the Library of Virginia in Richmond, and several FamilySearch collections covering Virginia's church, land, tax, and county court records from this era; because there was no national population count before 1790 and that first count was later destroyed, old tax lists stand in as the best substitute for knowing who lived where. Here is what the locality-guide found for New Orleans in the early 1800s:

---

**Locality Guide — New Orleans / Louisiana, 1800–1850**
*(Saved as loc_001)*

### Disaster Losses

Early-1800s New Orleans records were severely damaged or destroyed by:

- **Two major fires** — in **1788** and **1794** — which burned much of the French Quarter and wiped out many colonial-era documents.
- Ongoing losses from **yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods** throughout the period.

As a result, standard indexed civil birth, marriage, and death certificates don't exist for most of this era, and large portions of the paper trail are simply gone.

---

### What Survived — and Where to Look

| Record Type | Repository / Notes |
|---|---|
| **Catholic sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) | St. Louis Cathedral — records begin 1731, but with known gaps; heavily used as substitutes for civil registration |
| **Notarial acts** | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — dates to 1734; mostly on microfilm or in-person access only, not broadly searchable online |
| **Spanish colonial administrative records** | Cabildo government records (pre-1803) |
| **Succession records** (Louisiana's civil-law equivalent of probate/wills) | Generated by the French civil-law system; a valuable substitute when other records fail |

---

### A Note on the FamilySearch Wiki

The FamilySearch Wiki pages specifically covering New Orleans and Louisiana returned only a generic placeholder during this research pass. It is worth checking those pages directly for more detailed disaster-loss documentation before assuming nothing further is recorded.

---

In short: when records for early New Orleans are missing due to fires or floods, researchers should pivot to **Catholic church registers, notarial acts, and succession records** — the three pillars of the pre-statehood Louisiana paper trail that most often survived.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts (1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
Boston was a major Atlantic port and commercial center, and by the 1840s was experiencing a dramatic surge in immigration — particularly Irish Catholics fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852), who comprised over a quarter of Boston's residents by 1850.

---

## Immigration & Arrival Records

This is naturally the top priority for your research:

- **Customs Passenger Lists (1820–1891):** Record Group 36, National Archives. These 1840s manifests record name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — no later Ellis Island-era detail. Held physically at the **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)**.
- **FamilySearch collection 1784312** — "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (~1.23M people) — indexed and free.
- **Digitized volume 003345210** on FamilySearch: Port of Boston passenger lists, 1840–1850, 389 images, **full-text searchable but only ~3% name-indexed**. Use full-text search rather than name search for this volume to avoid missing entries.
- Also available on Ancestry.com per the FamilySearch Wiki.

---

## Church Records

For Irish Catholic immigrants especially:

- **FamilySearch collection 1921657** — "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (~988K people) — covers baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- Original parish registers at the **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's) per the FamilySearch Wiki ["Massachusetts Church Records"](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston).
- Church registers often fill gaps where civil vital records don't yet cover an event.

---

## Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **FamilySearch collection 2061550** — "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (~3.46M people) — covers the 1840s.

---

## Naturalization Records

- **FamilySearch collection 1459213** — "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (~346K people) — declarations and petitions that often followed a Boston arrival; can corroborate identity and date of immigration.

---

## Census Records

- **1840 and 1850 U.S. Federal Censuses** apply; Ancestry.com hosts the [U.S. Federal Census Collection](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

---

## Probate Records

- **FamilySearch collection 1678901** — "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (~568K people) — useful to confirm family relationships.

---

## Newspaper Records

- **The Pilot** (Boston Irish Catholic newspaper) published arrival notices and **missing-persons advertisements** specifically targeting separated immigrant families — a highly valuable source for Irish arrivals of the 1840s.
- Also check [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) and [Chronicling America](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/).

---

## Cemetery Records

- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) for Boston-area burials.

---

## Military Records

- [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) and [NARA](https://www.archives.gov/) for service and pension records (Mexican-American War, 1846–1848, falls within this window).

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Key Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (free) | Passenger lists, church records, vital records, naturalizations, probate | Free |
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham) | Original customs passenger lists, RG 36 | Physical |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers | Physical |
| Ancestry.com | Federal censuses, passenger lists | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Newspaper notices | Subscription |
| Fold3 / NARA | Military records | Varies |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with FamilySearch passenger lists** (collection 1784312 and volume 003345210). Because the 1840–1850 volume is only 3% name-indexed, **use full-text search** — a standard name search will miss most entries.
2. **1840s manifests are brief** — expect only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin; not the detail found in later records.
3. **Follow with Catholic parish registers** (Archdiocese archives and collection 1921657) — Irish immigrants of this era were overwhelmingly Catholic, and church registers often provide birth/marriage/death information not yet captured by civil registration.
4. **Search The Pilot newspaper** for missing-persons ads — these frequently named the immigrant's townland of origin in Ireland, a crucial clue for tracing ancestors back to their home parish.
5. After confirming an arrival, check **naturalization records** (collection 1459213) for the declaration of intent and petition, which can confirm arrival date, port, and country of origin.

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (mid-1800s, c. 1840–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Oklahoma did not exist as a state during the mid-1800s — that land was **Indian Territory**, administered directly by the federal government. The area became a U.S. state only in 1907. The Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole) were relocated there following the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and the Trail of Tears. No standard county courthouse structure existed; records run through federal Indian agencies, the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), and tribal governments.

> **Important:** Always search under **"Indian Territory"** as the place name — not a modern Oklahoma county — when working in pre-1907 collections.

---

## Key Record Types

### 🗂️ Tribal Rolls & Censuses *(primary source for this period)*

| Record | Date | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Old Settler Cherokee Roll | 1851 | Named in FamilySearch Wiki, "Oklahoma Native American Records" |
| Drennen Roll (Cherokee) | 1852 | Named in same FamilySearch Wiki article |
| Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 | 1851–1959 | FamilySearch collection id **1987432**, ~567,890 persons |
| Tribal Enrollment Cards (digitized volume) | 1840–1870 | FamilySearch image group **002298871**, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable — **best starting point** |
| Dawes Rolls | 1898–1914 | Allotment-era rolls; useful as cross-reference back to earlier family units; held at NARA Fort Worth and indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry |

### ⛪ Mission & Church Records

Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries worked among the relocated tribes from the 1820s onward, keeping registers of converts and community members.

- **FamilySearch:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" — collection id **1654321**, ~123,456 persons

### 🏞️ Land Records

Land in Indian Territory was tribally held under treaty, not distributed through the standard federal rectangular-survey system.

- **FamilySearch:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" — collection id **1541872**, ~234,567 persons — covers the full target window

### 📜 Treaty & Agency Records

- Annual annuity payment rolls, BIA correspondence, and school records are held at the **National Archives (NARA)**.
- Not confirmed as digitized online beyond the tribal enrollment cards volume above.
- Plan for an archival request or in-person visit to NARA, particularly the **Fort Worth facility**.

### ⛏️ Military Records

Some tribal members served in Civil War–era Indian Home Guard or Confederate Indian units; no specific FamilySearch collection was confirmed by this survey — a gap to investigate.

### 🪦 Cemetery / Probate / Vital Records

- **No civil vital registration** existed in Indian Territory before statehood (1907) — tribal rolls and mission registers are the substitute.
- Probate jurisdiction lay with tribal courts and councils, not U.S. county courts; no specific digitized probate series was confirmed for this period.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Tribal Enrollment Cards (vol. 002298871); Indian Censuses & Rolls, 1851–1959 (id 1987432); Mission & Church Records, 1820–1965 (id 1654321); Land Records, 1834–1907 (id 1541872) | Free — https://www.familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry** | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records | Subscription |
| **NARA (National Archives) — Fort Worth** | Dawes Rolls originals; annuity rolls; BIA agency correspondence; treaty records | In-person or NARA request — https://www.archives.gov/ |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start** with FamilySearch's digitized Tribal Enrollment Cards (image group **002298871**) — it is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable, making it the fastest entry point for the mid-1800s.
2. **Search the Indian Censuses & Rolls collection** (id 1987432), which directly covers the 1851 Old Settler Cherokee Roll and 1852 Drennen Roll.
3. **Cross-check mission registers** (id 1654321) — Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries recorded tribal community members from the 1820s onward.
4. **Plan an archival step** for treaty and agency records (BIA correspondence, annuity rolls) — these are described in the FamilySearch Wiki as held at the National Archives and are not confirmed online.
5. **Search under "Indian Territory"** as the place name, not a modern Oklahoma county, since Oklahoma only resolves from 1907 onward in most tools and databases.
6. Use the Dawes Rolls (Ancestry and NARA, 1898–1914) as a *cross-reference* back to earlier family units, even though they postdate the mid-1800s target window.

---

## Known Gaps in This Survey

- The FamilySearch Wiki's Oklahoma-specific "home" and "vital records" pages returned only generic template content and could not be fully retrieved; there may be additional official Wiki guidance that this survey did not capture.
- No specific digitized Civil War–era military records for Indian Territory tribal units were confirmed.
- Digitization levels for the mission/church records collection (id 1654321) were not fully confirmed beyond the collection listing itself.

---

The next step would be to build a research plan starting with the tribal-roll collections on FamilySearch, then plan an archival request to NARA Fort Worth for agency and treaty records not yet digitized.

- **What exists:** The Bureau of Indian Affairs maintained agency records — annuity payment rolls, correspondence, and school records — now held at the National Archives (FamilySearch Wiki, "Oklahoma Native American Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records). - **Federal census:** Indian Territory residents were largely excluded from the regular federal decennial census in this period; the tribal rolls above are the substitute enumeration. This survey did not confirm a specific federal Indian Territory census schedule.

## Research tips
- Start with FamilySearch's digitized Tribal Enrollment Cards volume (image group 002298871), which is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable — the fastest path into this period.

This survey covered the area that became Oklahoma, focused on the mid-1800s, when it was not a U.S. state but "Indian Territory," land where the federal government relocated the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole nations. For this period the key records are not courthouse birth or marriage certificates but tribal rolls and censuses (such as the 1851 Old Settler Cherokee Roll and 1852 Drennen Roll, plus a large indexed set of tribal enrollment cards), along with mission church registers, land records, and federal treaty and agency papers, most of which are either digitized and searchable on FamilySearch or held physically at the National Archives, including its Fort Worth location. The locality guide is complete and saved as **loc_001**. Here is the survey:

---

**Pennsylvania Quaker Records — Late 1700s**

Quaker monthly meeting records are the cornerstone for tracing Pennsylvania Friends families in this period. The Religious Society of Friends recorded **births, marriages, deaths, removals (moves), and disciplinary actions** in their own meeting minutes long before Pennsylvania required civil registration (which did not begin until 1906). Key points from the survey:

**What to Search**
- **Monthly meeting minutes and registers** — record births, marriages, disownments, certificates of removal, and deaths. These are organized by meeting, not county.
- **Certificates of removal** — issued when a member moved to another meeting, essential for tracing migration.
- **Disownment records** — note members who married outside the faith or otherwise violated discipline; they still name the person.

**Primary Repositories**
- **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** — the largest single repository of Pennsylvania Quaker records.
- **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** — major holdings, especially Philadelphia-area meetings.
- **FamilySearch** — a digitized volume of **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes (1750–1800)** is available, but it is **browse-only** (no name index), so it requires page-by-page reading.

**Densest Quaker Areas in Pennsylvania**
Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties had the highest Quaker concentration in the late 1700s.

**Reference Tool: Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy**
Before browsing unindexed FamilySearch volumes, check **Hinshaw's Encyclopedia** first — it indexes thousands of Quaker meeting records by name and is a major time-saver.

**A Note of Caution**
Some FamilySearch Wiki pages consulted during this survey returned generic placeholders rather than Pennsylvania-specific content. Details on land records, tax records, and exact repository access terms should be verified directly on the FamilySearch Research Wiki.

---

**Next step:** Once you identify a specific Quaker family and subject, the **research-plan** step can turn this guide into a concrete, sequenced search plan.

- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States.

- **Economy:** Not surveyed by tools in this run.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quaker settlers concentrated heavily in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties by the late 1700s (Wikipedia, "Quakers in Pennsylvania").
- **Religious denominations:** The Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) was a dominant denomination in these counties; other denominations existed but were not covered by this survey.
- **Key historical events:** Pennsylvania was founded explicitly as a Quaker haven in 1682, shaping the density and continuity of Quaker meeting records in the southeastern counties (Wikipedia, "Quakers in Pennsylvania").

## Boundary changes
This survey covered Pennsylvania at the state level only; no county-level boundary history was requested or surveyed. Quaker meetings are organized by meeting (Monthly/Quarterly/Yearly), not by civil county, so a county boundary change does not necessarily move a family's meeting records to a different repository — the Friends Historical Library and Swarthmore's holdings are organized by meeting name, not by current county.

- **Where held:** Not applicable for this period at the civil level.
- **Gaps:** Entire 1750-1800 window has no civil vital registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting minutes recorded births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal, and disownments, and substitute for the missing civil registration (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Church Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) is the denomination this survey targeted; Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties had particularly dense Quaker populations in the colonial and early national periods (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Church Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).

- **Where held:** The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College holds the largest collection of American Quaker records (Wikipedia, "Quakers in Pennsylvania"); the Quaker and Special Collections at Haverford College is also named by Wikipedia as a primary repository. Guide saved as **loc_001** (Allegheny County / Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, 1870–1900).

---

Here is what the survey found for tracing Pittsburgh families through occupational and industrial sources in the late 1800s:

## Strongest Starting Points

**City Directories (Free, Online)**
Pittsburgh city directories survive for most years in this period and routinely list each resident's trade or employer. Available free and full-text at the University of Pittsburgh's *Historic Pittsburgh* site, covering 1815–1930. These are often the fastest way to place an ancestor at a specific mill or factory.

**Federal Census Schedules (1880 & 1900)**
Both record occupation. The 1900 census also captures immigration year — useful for the many immigrant steel workers in Pittsburgh during this era.

## Company Personnel Records (Subscription)
Two Ancestry collections are worth targeting:
- **Westinghouse employment records**, 1890–1953
- **Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania records**, including Jones & Laughlin Steel Corporation material

## In-Person / Written-Request Archives
Mill, union, and factory-inspector records survive only in fragmentary, non-digitized form at:
- **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh)
- **Rivers of Steel archives**

These require a written request or in-person visit.

## Key Caveats for Vital Records
- County-level vital registration predates Pennsylvania's 1906 statewide mandate, so births, marriages, and deaths in this period are filed at the county level.
- Catholic parish registers were organized by **immigrant ethnicity**, not simple geography — identifying the correct ethnic parish is essential.
- Records before 1907 may appear under **"Allegheny City"** rather than "Pittsburgh," since the two were separate municipalities until annexation.

## Suggested Next Step
Build a research plan sequencing searches in this order:
1. Free, indexed marriage and mortality collections + city directories
2. Subscription company-records collections (Westinghouse, J&L)
3. Written request to Heinz History Center / Rivers of Steel for company and union records

- **Formed:** September 24, 1788, from Washington and Westmoreland Counties (FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy).

## Boundary changes

args.guideSection:
### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County/town-level birth and death registration 1852-54 and again 1893; county marriage licenses from 1885; statewide registration for births and deaths began January 1906, with general compliance by 1915 (Pennsylvania Vital Records, FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records). No statewide marriage registration date is given by that page.
- **What exists:** For 1870-1900, expect county-level birth/death records (where filed) and marriage licenses from 1885 onward; pre-1906 compliance was inconsistent, so coverage before 1906 is uneven.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Courthouse, 436 Grant St., Pittsburgh — Register of Wills holds marriage records, per the Allegheny County Genealogy page. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" (collection 1921317, 1,048,378 people) and "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 people) are indexed online, but the death collection only starts in 1906, outside most of this target window.
- **Gaps:** Before 1906, death and birth registration was inconsistent at the county level; no FamilySearch death-records collection covers 1870-1905 for this county per this survey's `collections_search` results.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church (parish) baptism, marriage, and burial registers, which the Allegheny County Genealogy page says are extensive and often ethnically organized.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic parishes serving specific ethnic communities — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish — per the Allegheny County Genealogy page and Wikipedia; other denominations not itemized by a tool result in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers.
- **Where held:** Individual parishes and the diocesan archive; the Allegheny County Genealogy page directs to a separate "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Church Records" wiki page for denomination-by-denomination detail, not fetched in this survey.
- **Gaps:** This survey did not confirm specific missing years or losses for any denomination; the dedicated church-records wiki page should be read for that detail.
- **Language:** Not stated by a tool result for Allegheny County specifically; expect some registers in Polish, Slovak, Croatian, or Italian given the parishes' ethnic organization, but this is inferred from population composition, not a records page.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, 1890 (largely destroyed by fire, a nationwide 1890 loss not specific to this county), and 1900 federal censuses apply to this window; the 1880 and 1900 schedules record occupation, and 1900 also records immigration year, per the wiki_search result on Allegheny County Census and Naturalization.
- **State/provincial census:** None confirmed by this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880 (FamilySearch collection 3512181) overlap part of this period.
- **Access:** University of Pittsburgh hosts digitized/searchable census name indexes, but only for Allegheny City (1850, 1860, 1870) and Pittsburgh proper (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) — no coverage for the rest of the county's boroughs/townships, per the Allegheny County Genealogy page.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianship (Orphan's Court), adoptions/name changes.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not known for a specific ancestor; search both will (testate) and administration (intestate) series at the courthouse.
- **Date range:** County probate and court records run from 1788, per the Allegheny County Genealogy page's records-dates table; FamilySearch's "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196) covers the state but shows 0 indexed people in this survey's `collections_search` result — effectively browse-only for name search.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Courthouse (Clerk of Courts holds probate and court records; Register of Wills handles marriages; Prothonotary handles divorce, per the Allegheny County Genealogy page).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not stated by a tool result in this survey.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** County Recorder of Deeds holds land records from 1788, per the Allegheny County Genealogy page's records-dates table.
- **Types:** Deeds; specific grant/patent detail not confirmed by this survey (the county-specific Land and Property wiki page was not fetched).
- **Date range:** From 1788.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** None specific to 1870-1900 Allegheny County confirmed by a tool result in this survey (no major US war fell inside this window; Civil War and Spanish-American War veterans' later pension files may still be relevant).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files — held at the National Archives per general U.S. practice; no Allegheny-County-specific military collection was returned by this survey's tools.
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA); state adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives (not itemized by a tool result here).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery is named specifically by the Allegheny County Genealogy page, with its own online name-search tool.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave, BillionGraves, PAGenWeb Archives, PA-Roots, and FamilySearch's "Pennsylvania, Pittsburgh, Allegheny Cemetery Records, 1845-1960" (collection 3155912, index only) and "Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950" (collection 3743478, index & images), per the Allegheny County Genealogy page.
- **Physical records:** Sexton/burial registers at individual cemeteries; FamilySearch's cemetery abstracts collection is noted as incomplete.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Not itemized by name or date range by any tool result in this survey.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by this survey; the external-links search did return Newspapers.com as a general resource.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices are standard newspaper genealogical content, but no Pittsburgh-specific title/date range was returned here.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Pittsburgh is inland; the Allegheny County Genealogy page points instead to naturalization records at the county courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia, and Pennsylvania-wide "Landing Reports of Aliens, 1798-1828" (collection 1908383) — predating this period.
- **Record types:** Naturalization declarations and petitions (Court of Common Pleas, Allegheny County, 1798-1930 per a `wiki_search` result); passenger lists at NARA for the actual port of arrival (commonly New York, not Pittsburgh).
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records are held at the National Archives at Philadelphia, per a `wiki_search` result on Census and Naturalization.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants traveling with parents — check the full manifest for all family members once the port and ship are identified.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Not itemized specifically for Allegheny County by a tool result in this survey.
- **Date range:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by this survey; likely county-held per general Pennsylvania practice, but no page named one.
- **Substitute value:** Could substitute for the lost/partial 1890 federal census, but this survey found no tax-record collection to name specifically.

### Other record types
- **Occupational/industrial records:** "Pennsylvania, U.S. Westinghouse Employment Records, 1890-1953" (Ancestry collection 63266, index & images, subscription) and "Pennsylvania U.S., Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania, 1890-1973" (Ancestry collection 62557, index & images, subscription; includes Jones & Laughlin Steel Corporation records) — both from the Allegheny County Genealogy page's Business, Commerce, and Occupations section. A `wiki_search` result also notes fragmentary company employment records at the Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel archives, union membership lists, and Pennsylvania state factory inspector reports, none of which this survey could cite to a specific online collection.
- **City directories:** Pittsburgh directories exist from the 1810s onward; the Allegheny County Genealogy page's "Don's List" names extant years including 1864-65, 1867, 1872, 1875, 1877-79, 1884-85, 1890, 1895, and 1897-1903 — directly spanning this period and listing occupations — plus a Historic Pittsburgh full-text collection (1815-1930) at the University of Pittsburgh and Fold3's Pittsburgh City Directories (1861-1923, subscription). Directories are a prime occupational source since 19th-century directories routinely list each resident's trade or employer.

|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Courthouse, 436 Grant St., Pittsburgh, PA 15219 | Marriage records (Register of Wills), probate and court records (Clerk of Courts/Court Records Director), land records (Recorder of Deeds), divorce records (Prothonotary) | In person or by mail; (412) 350-6500 |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records, 1798-1930 | In person or by request |

| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Original ethnic-parish baptism, marriage, burial registers | By request to the diocese |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1906 Allegheny County death records are not confirmed as an online indexed/image collection by this survey.
