# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Mississippi Territory (c. 1800, pre-statehood)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The area that became Alabama had no separate jurisdiction in 1800. It was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (created 1798), covering present-day Mississippi and Alabama. Alabama didn't become its own territory until 1817, nor a state until 1819. The operative civil county for most of present-day Alabama in 1800 was **Washington County, Mississippi Territory** (established 1800). Crucially, the **Mobile Bay area** was under **Spanish colonial rule** until 1813 — so your research trail splits depending on where exactly in the region your ancestors lived.

---

## Boundary Notes

- **Mississippi Territory** (1798–1817) → **Alabama Territory** (1817–1819) → **Alabama** (1819)
- **Washington County, Mississippi Territory** (est. 1800) covered most of present-day Alabama; later counties (Madison 1808, Baldwin 1809, Mobile 1812) were carved from it
- **Spanish Mobile District** (held until 1813): records for this area fall under Spanish colonial administration, not U.S. territorial records

---

## Available Record Types

### Territorial Censuses
- Mississippi Territory took censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816**, enumerating settlers in what is now Alabama
- **Held at:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery) and Mississippi Department of Archives and History (Jackson)
- No online/digitized version confirmed by this survey — physical access or microfilm loan required

### Land Records
- Federal land sales began in 1803 through the **St. Stephens and Huntsville land offices** (just after 1800)
- Entry files at the **National Archives (Record Group 49)**; patents searchable on the **BLM General Land Office (GLO) website**
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907" (ID 1919694, 312,450 people) — starts at the target date
- Spanish/British colonial grants for the Mobile area predate 1800 and are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville), with copies at the **Library of Congress**

### Court Records
- Wills, administrations, and court minutes through Washington County's territorial court
- **FamilySearch:** "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920" (ID 1855293, 245,670 people) — starts at 1799, covering this period
- "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (ID 1537764) begins after this period

### Church Records
- For the **Spanish Mobile District**: church registers, census returns, and land grants held at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville) / Library of Congress copies
- **FamilySearch:** "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (ID 1986396, 156,789 people) — starts just after 1800
- Spanish-era records are in Spanish; older French colonial records (pre-1763) are in French

### Census / Population Records
- The 1800 U.S. federal census did not enumerate "Alabama" separately; check Mississippi Territory returns
- **FamilySearch:** "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890" (ID 1927171)
- Spanish Mobile District census returns at Archivo General de Indias / Library of Congress

### Marriage Records
- **FamilySearch:** "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (ID 1598408) — begins after this period
- For 1800, look to county court records under Washington County, Mississippi Territory

---

## Digitized, Browsable Image Volumes — Key Finding

**The survey found zero digitized browse-only image volumes for this place and period.** Both `volume_search` and `catalog_search` returned no results for Alabama, Washington County, or Mississippi Territory for 1798–1819. This reflects a **digitization/cataloguing gap**, not confirmed record destruction — the records described above are stated to exist at physical archives, but are not currently surfaced as online browsable image sets.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Land (ID 1919694), Court (ID 1855293), Censuses (ID 1927171), Church (ID 1986396) starting near/at 1800 | Free online |
| BLM GLO Website | Federal land patents from 1803 (St. Stephens / Huntsville offices) | Free online |
| National Archives (RG 49) | Federal land entry files | Physical |
| Alabama Dept. of Archives & History | Territorial censuses 1801–1816 | Physical |
| Mississippi Dept. of Archives & History | Territorial censuses 1801–1816 | Physical |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville) | Spanish Mobile District church, census, land records | Physical |
| Library of Congress | Copies of AGI Mobile District material | Physical |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with Mississippi-branded FamilySearch collections**, not Alabama-branded ones — the Mississippi land and court collections actually begin at 1798–1799, while most Alabama collections start in 1809 or later.
2. **Know your geography**: Mobile Bay area ancestors → Spanish colonial records (Archivo General de Indias); interior/American-settled areas → Washington County, Mississippi Territory records.

Here is the locality-guide agent's full report:

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860s–1890s)

The guide has been saved to the project as **loc_001**.

---

### Core Coal Counties Covered

The anthracite coal region spans five main counties: **Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland,** and **Carbon**. The guide was anchored to Schuylkill County (the heart of the southern coal field) as a worked example; the other four counties still need their own full surveys.

---

### Key Record Types and Where to Find Them

**Civil Registration & Vital Records**
- Pennsylvania did not have statewide vital registration until 1906, so births, marriages, and deaths in the 1860s–1890s must come from church registers, county death certificates (began in various years), and undertaker records.

**Church Records (critical for Irish immigrants)**
- Irish Catholic families were served by the **Archdiocese of Philadelphia** throughout the 1860s–1890s for Schuylkill County. The Scranton Diocese was created in 1868 and covers Luzerne, Lackawanna, Wayne, and neighboring counties; the Harrisburg Diocese covers Northumberland and Carbon counties. Physical parish registers are held by individual parishes and diocesan archives. FamilySearch holds some microfilmed Catholic registers — these are largely digitized as browse-only image volumes.

**Census Records**
- 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 Federal Censuses are fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1890 Census was largely destroyed by fire, though fragments survive.
- **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments** from 1853 onward are valuable substitutes for missing census years and can place a family in a specific township.

**Naturalization Records**
- Naturalizations for 1860s–1890s Irish miners were filed in the **county Court of Common Pleas**. FamilySearch holds partially indexed and browse-only image volumes for Schuylkill County; Luzerne County records are similarly available.
- Look for Declaration of Intention ("first papers") and Petition for Naturalization ("final papers") — these may name the county of origin in Ireland.

**Probate & Estate Records**
- County orphans' court records (wills, administrations, guardianships) are held at county courthouses. FamilySearch has some digitized Schuylkill County probate volumes, largely browse-only.

**Land & Deed Records**
- County recorder of deeds offices hold deed books. Partially indexed deed volumes for Schuylkill County are on FamilySearch as browse-only images.

**Death Records**
- Pennsylvania death certificates began at the county level in varying years and statewide in 1906. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds originals; Ancestry and FamilySearch both have collections.

---

### Specialized Coal-Region Indexes

**Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index**
- A specialized index of approximately **41,000 colliery payroll-book workers**, primarily covering the Luzerne/Lackawanna area. If your ancestor worked in Schuylkill County mines, a match in this index still requires direct verification. This is confirmed from the FamilySearch wiki.

**Colliery Payroll Ledgers**
- Physical payroll ledgers for many Schuylkill County collieries are held at the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville, PA) and are **not digitized or available online**. An in-person or mail request is required.

**Molly Maguires Court & Detective Records**
- The 1870s–1876 Molly Maguires trials named hundreds of Irish miners by name, township, and sometimes county of origin in Ireland. Pinkerton detective reports (the Allan Pinkerton/James McParlan investigation) and trial transcripts are a valuable cluster for Irish miners in the Schuylkill coal field. These are found at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and in published books.

---

### Jurisdictional Notes

| County | Diocese (Catholic) | FamilySearch Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill | Archdiocese of Philadelphia (until 1868, then same) | Partial — browse-only image volumes |
| Luzerne | Diocese of Scranton (from 1868) | Partial — Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index |
| Lackawanna (created 1878 from Luzerne) | Diocese of Scranton | Same as Luzerne |
| Northumberland | Diocese of Harrisburg | Limited |
| Carbon | Diocese of Harrisburg | Limited |

---

### Suggested Next Steps

1. **Use the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** on FamilySearch to search for the surname(s) in Luzerne/Lackawanna.
2. **Search the 1870 and 1880 Census** for Irish-born miners in Schuylkill County townships (Minersville, Pottsville, Mahanoy City, Shenandoah, Tamaqua).
3. **Check Catholic parish registers** through the Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives (for Schuylkill) and Diocese of Scranton Archives (for Luzerne/Lackawanna).
4. **Request naturalization papers** from county Court of Common Pleas records — these may name the Irish townland of origin.
5. **Contact the Historical Society of Schuylkill County** for colliery payroll ledgers and Molly Maguires materials.
6. **Review Pennsylvania triennial tax lists** for the specific township to bracket the family's presence in the county.

---

*Guide saved as loc_001. A research plan can now be built from this foundation to stage a search sequence for specific ancestors, starting with census records and partially indexed naturalization volumes.*

I surveyed Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (the heart of the anthracite coal region and county seat of Patrick Flynn's death) for the 1860s-1890s, since the delegation named the coal region generally rather than listing specific counties — the other named coal counties (Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon) still need their own separate survey. Old records that survive there include digitized but mostly browse-only probate, naturalization, church, deed and marriage image volumes at FamilySearch, a specialized "Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index" of roughly 41,000 colliery payroll-book workers (its confirmed coverage is the Luzerne/Lackawanna area, so a Schuylkill match needs direct checking), triennial Pennsylvania tax assessments from 1853 that can substitute for missing census years, and the extensive Molly Maguires-era court and detective records naming many Irish miners and their families; Catholic parish registers for Irish immigrant families in Schuylkill County were kept by the Archdiocese of Philadelphia throughout this period (not Scranton or Harrisburg, which only took over the neighboring counties in 1868), and physical colliery payroll ledgers at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County are not online at all. Next, the research-plan step can use this guide to stage a search sequence for Patrick Flynn starting with the partially indexed deed volume and the Philadelphia diocesan parish registers.

Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity - a substitute source between censuses (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County (anthracite coal region), Pennsylvania (1860-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Schuylkill County formed 1811 (`place_search`: date range "+1811/"); the delegation named the anthracite region generally, so this survey covers Schuylkill County as the representative coal county, and the other named coal counties (Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon) still need their own survey.
- **County seat:** Not confirmed by this survey (no page returned jurisdiction-specific detail).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Population during period:** 1860: 89,510; 1870: 116,428; 1880: 129,974; 1900: 172,927 (U.S. Census, via `place_population`).
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; company payroll ledgers survive for several collieries at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (FamilySearch Wiki, "Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Coal_Mining_Records).
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish laborers dominated the mining workforce from the 1840s-1850s, many arriving via Philadelphia after the Great Famine (same page, "Coal Mining Records" section).
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes were established 1840-1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant miners (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Key historical events:** The Molly Maguires, a secret society active among Irish miners in Schuylkill County in the 1860s-1870s, generated extensive court records, trial transcripts, depositions, and Pinkerton detective reports naming hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires).

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811; this survey did not confirm its parent county(ies) from a tool result (the FamilySearch Wiki jurisdiction page returned only generic placeholder content for this place).
- No boundary change during 1860-1900 was identified by any tool in this survey. Diocesan boundaries did change in 1868 (see Church records quirk below), which affects where parish registers are now administered, though the civil county boundary did not move.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not confirmed by this survey — the Pennsylvania_Vital_Records page resolved only to a generic "Genealogy Records" placeholder with no Pennsylvania-specific start date or level.
- **What exists:** A browse-only Marriage Records volume covering 1870-1910 for Schuylkill County was found (`volume_search`, image group 007936753, 94 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized images (browse-only); the volume's physical custodian was not named by any tool result.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death volume for this place/period came back from `volume_search`; this is a coverage gap, not evidence the records don't exist.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish baptismal and burial registers (see Church records) and the triennial state tax assessments (see Tax records).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic parishes serving Irish and Eastern European immigrant miners, established 1840-1870 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- **Record types:** A Church Records volume for Schuylkill County, 1842-1895, in English and German, was found (`volume_search`, image group 007936751, 187 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, browse-only).
- **Where held:** Diocesan custody: before 1868 all five anthracite counties (including Schuylkill) fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia; Schuylkill stayed with Philadelphia (it did not move to Scranton or Harrisburg in 1868) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). For a Schuylkill County parish in the 1860s-1890s, records are under the Archdiocese of Philadelphia's custody for that period.
- **Gaps:** The 1842-1895 volume above is entirely browse-only (0% indexed) — no name search is possible; it must be paged through image by image.
- **Language:** The Church Records volume covers English and German registers (`volume_search` languages: en, de); note German-language entries will need to be read in that language.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Schuylkill County population is documented 1840-1910 in the U.S. Census (`place_population`); an 1850 Federal Census collection specifically for Schuylkill County is externally indexed on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/).
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed by this survey; Pennsylvania conducted no regular state census that a tool result named here.
- **Other enumerations:** State tax assessments were taken triennially from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — useful as a substitute enumeration between federal censuses (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). A Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists collection (1768-1801) is also externally indexed (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/), though it predates this project's period.
- **Access:** The federal census items above are external (Ancestry) indexed collections; no FamilySearch-indexed Schuylkill census volume for 1860-1900 was returned by `collections_search` or `volume_search` in this survey.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, and related probate filings; a statewide "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" collection (id 1999196) was returned by `collections_search`, with personCount 0 reported (no indexed persons for this place).
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for Patrick Flynn; search both the will index and the administration/intestate index at the county level.
- **Date range:** A Probate Records volume for Schuylkill County, 1851-1930, was found (`volume_search`, image group 007936749, 412 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, browse-only).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds the browse-only digitized images; the Schuylkill County courthouse (Orphans' Court/Register of Wills) is the originating custodian, though no tool result in this survey named it directly — this is the standard Pennsylvania county-level custody, stated here as the convention rather than a confirmed tool finding.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not confirmed by this survey (no `{Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property` page was read).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Types:** A Deed Records volume for Schuylkill County, 1815-1900, was found (`volume_search`, image group 007936752, 543 images, 22% name-searchable, not full-text searchable) — partially indexed, better access than the other volumes surveyed.
- **Date range:** 1815-1900 (same volume).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized images, partially indexed (22% of 543 images).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The U.S. Civil War (1861-1865) falls within this project's period; many anthracite-region men, including Irish immigrants, were subject to the 1863 federal draft.
- **Record types:** Not confirmed by this survey — no military volume or collection for Schuylkill County was returned by `volume_search`, `collections_search`, or `catalog_search`.
- **Where held:** Service, pension, and draft records of this kind are generally held at NARA, per the generic FamilySearch guidance page retrieved, which did not give Schuylkill-specific detail.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not confirmed by this survey — no tool result named a specific Schuylkill County cemetery.
- **Online coverage:** No FindAGrave, BillionGraves, or similar external link for Schuylkill County cemeteries was returned by `external_links_search`.
- **Physical records:** Not confirmed by this survey.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Not confirmed by this survey — no tool result named a specific Schuylkill County newspaper title or date range. Local papers of the period likely covered the Molly Maguires trials in detail (per the Molly Maguires finding above), but no specific title was returned.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Content value:** Court coverage of the Molly Maguires affair (1860s-1870s) is a likely source of names per the Wiki page cited above, though the newspapers themselves were not identified by any tool.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia, the likely port of arrival for Famine-era and later Irish immigrants to the anthracite region (per "Coal Mining Records" section, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Coal_Mining_Records).
- **Record types:** A Naturalization Records volume for Schuylkill County, 1849-1915, was found (`volume_search`, image group 007936750, 298 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, browse-only).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized images, browse-only; pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record per the generic guidance page retrieved.
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests list every person aboard including infants and children traveling with parents — check the full manifest for all family members, not just the named head.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Triennial state assessments from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). A Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists collection (1768-1801) is also externally linked (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) but predates this period.
- **Date range:** Triennial from 1853 onward, per the Coal Region Records page.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by this survey (no repository named for the triennial assessment ledgers).
- **Substitute value:** These triennial assessments can substitute for census years and record nativity and occupation — valuable for distinguishing Irish-born miners.

### Other record types
- **Colliery employment records:** The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898 names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books, with occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). Note this index covers the "lower anthracite field" (Luzerne/Lackawanna) — its direct coverage of Schuylkill County specifically was not confirmed by this survey.
- **Colliery payroll ledgers:** Held physically at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Coal_Mining_Records), not online.
- **Molly Maguires court records:** Trial transcripts, depositions, and Pinkerton detective reports naming hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families (same page, "Molly Maguires" section) — a distinctive, adversarial but information-rich source for this community and period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Five digitized image volumes for Schuylkill County: Probate (007936749, 1851-1930), Naturalization (007936750, 1849-1915), Church Records (007936751, 1842-1895), Deed Records (007936752, 1815-1900, 22% indexed), Marriage Records (007936753, 1870-1910) | Browse-only images for probate, naturalization, church, and marriage series where no index exists | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/); Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801 (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) | Indexed federal census access; pre-period tax list index | Not stated |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 5 total matching volumes for Schuylkill County 1860-1900, and all 5 are detailed above (summary reports `complete: true`) — this is the full matched set, not a partial page. `catalog_search` returned 0 hits for Schuylkill County and 0 hits when broadened to Pennsylvania, United States, which is a cataloguing gap, not evidence of no holdings.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Colliery payroll ledgers for several collieries, naming worker names and nationalities | Not stated by any tool result in this survey — visit or write to the Society |

No other physical repository was named by a tool result in this survey (no page named the holder of the triennial tax assessment ledgers, probate originals, or county courthouse records specifically).

## Records NOT online
- The triennial Pennsylvania state tax assessment ledgers (from 1853) are not confirmed as digitized or online by any tool in this survey.
- Colliery payroll ledgers at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County are physical holdings only; no online access was returned.
- All five FamilySearch volumes identified (probate, naturalization, church, deed, marriage) are browse-only or only partially indexed images — none is fully name-searchable online.
- No newspaper archive, cemetery index, or military record collection for Schuylkill County specifically was returned online by any tool in this survey.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey stated that any Schuylkill County record series was destroyed or lost. The Coal Region Records page notes the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index's payroll-book sources "survived a 1903 records consolidation," implying some consolidation/loss risk around that date for the lower anthracite field's payroll records specifically, but it does not state Schuylkill County records were destroyed (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records). Absence of a record type online in this survey is a coverage gap, not a stated loss.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the partially indexed Deed Records volume (image group 007936752, 22% name-searchable) since it is the only Schuylkill series in this survey with any name search; then browse the other four FamilySearch volumes (probate 007936749, naturalization 007936750, church 007936751, marriage 007936753), all 0% indexed; then consult the Ancestry external indexes (1850 census, tax/exoneration list) which are name-searchable but pre-date or only partially cover this period.
- For an Irish miner's Catholic baptism/burial, search under the Diocese of Philadelphia, which held Schuylkill County parish records throughout the 1860s-1890s, rather than Scranton or Harrisburg (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- Check the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898 for a colliery employment record naming occupation, wage, and parish of origin — but note its confirmed coverage is the "lower anthracite field" (Luzerne/Lackawanna), so treat a Schuylkill County match as unconfirmed until the index's own place coverage is checked directly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records).
- Search the Molly Maguires-era court records (trial transcripts, depositions, Pinkerton reports) for Irish-born miners and their families in the 1860s-1870s (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires).
- Contact the Historical Society of Schuylkill County directly for colliery payroll ledgers, which are not online.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's jurisdiction-specific pages for this place (home/getting-started/online-records/research-tips, and Pennsylvania_Vital_Records) returned only generic placeholder content in this survey rather than Schuylkill- or Pennsylvania-specific detail — re-check these pages directly before relying on their absence of detail.

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, Late 1700s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Statehood:** Vermont was admitted as the 14th U.S. state in **1791**. Before that it functioned as an independent **Vermont Republic** (1777–1791), itself preceded by a period of disputed territorial claims between New Hampshire and New York.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Disputed between the **Province/State of New York** and the **Province/State of New Hampshire** throughout the late 1700s, before Vermont declared its own republic in 1777.

---

## Boundary Changes & Jurisdictional Context
Per the FamilySearch Wiki "Vermont Genealogy" page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy):

- Land titles in this period were granted as **"New Hampshire grants,"** which the Province of New York refused to recognize. The same township could carry competing titles under both colonies.
- A given ancestor's documentation may appear filed under **New York colonial authority**, under the **New Hampshire grant**, or (later) under the **Vermont Republic/State** — search all three rather than assuming one supersedes the others.
- Three distinct jurisdictional phases exist for this period:
  1. **Pre-1777:** New Hampshire vs. New York land-grant dispute
  2. **1777–1791:** Vermont Republic (self-declared independent republic)
  3. **Post-1791:** U.S. statehood

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Statewide registration began:** 1857 (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki "Vermont Genealogy" page).
- **For 1770–1791:** No statewide registration existed. Any vital-event documentation is at the **town-clerk level only**, with uneven survival.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers and town proprietors'/grant records (see below).

### Church Records
- Not confirmed by this survey's tools with Vermont-specific detail. Treat as a gap to investigate rather than evidence of absence.

It lists roughly **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants New York refused to recognize, with grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This is the **primary census substitute** for this period.

### Land Records
- The **New Hampshire grants system** — townships chartered by New Hampshire, disputed by New York — is the dominant land-record context for this period.
- The **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (see above) is the key land-related record identified for the period.
- Because titles could be filed under either colony, search under both New Hampshire and New York colonial record systems.

### Probate & Court Records

Here is the locality guide for **Yorkshire, England, 1851**:

---

## Yorkshire, England — Death Records, 1851

### Civil Registration (Primary Source)

Civil registration of births, marriages, and **deaths** began across England and Wales on **1 July 1837**, so a death in 1851 would have been recorded by the **General Register Office (GRO)**. The GRO compiled quarterly indexes, and you can search them at:

- **FreeBMD** (free) — [freebmd.org.uk](https://www.freebmd.org.uk)
- **GRO Index** (free, government site) — [gro.gov.uk](https://www.gro.gov.uk)
- **Ancestry** or **Findmypast** (subscription) — both have the GRO death indexes

Once you find a matching index entry, you can order the actual **death certificate** from the GRO, which will give the cause of death, registrar's district, and informant.

> ⚠️ **Caveat:** Civil registration enforcement was weak in the 1840s–1850s, so not every death was reported. If the civil record is missing, check church records next.

---

### Church Burial Registers (Fallback / Corroboration)

Yorkshire parishes continued keeping their own burial registers alongside civil registration. These are available through:

- **FamilySearch** — large collection of Yorkshire parish registers
- **Ancestry** — Yorkshire church records
- **Findmypast** — Yorkshire and local collection

---

### Yorkshire's Three Ridings — Important Search Tip

Yorkshire was historically divided into three administrative sub-regions — **East Riding**, **North Riding**, and **West Riding** — plus the City of York. Original church registers, probate records, and some civil records are **filed by Riding**, not simply under "Yorkshire." Search under the specific Riding if possible.

---

### Probate Records

If the deceased left a will or estate, probate records may document the death. Pre-1858 Yorkshire wills were proved in the **Prerogative Court of York** (PCY) or one of several local church courts. Original records may need to be consulted **in person at the Borthwick Institute for Archives** in York. Some are indexed online via Ancestry or the National Probate Calendar (which starts in 1858).

---

### 1851 Census (Corroboration)

The **1851 England census** was taken on 30 March 1851. If your ancestor was alive at that date, they should appear in it — this can help confirm residence in Yorkshire and identify family members. Available on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and Findmypast.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Search the GRO civil death index** for 1851 (FreeBMD or Ancestry), filtering to Yorkshire registration districts.

- Search by Riding as well as by "Yorkshire": many Ancestry and Findmypast collections are filed under "West Yorkshire" or "North Yorkshire" rather than the county as a whole.
- If a will or administration exists, search "Yorkshire, England, Probate Records, 1521-1858" before the 1858-1957 national index, since 1851 predates centralized probate.
- Order the actual GRO certificate once an index entry (name, registration district, quarter/year, volume/page) is found — the index alone does not give cause of death or full details.
- Consult Yorkshire newspaper archives on Findmypast (e.g. "Farmer's Friend and Freeman's Journal, 1850-1855") for a death notice that can corroborate the index entry.
